speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EFFECT UPON MEN EMPLOYED ON DAY LABOUR BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 1 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked if the government would consider the advisability, in making proclamation of a holiday for any purpose, of providing that such holiday shall be with pay. I replied at the time that the government had not had an opportunity to give special attention to the question beyond that which it had received at different times, but that we would give further consideration to it.
My reply to-day is that the government is advised that under the constitution the jurisdiction of parliament to legislate generally in respect of holidays does not enable parliament to impose upon employers liability to pay wages to persons employed on a day labour basis at an hourly rate of payment, in respect of holidays observed as such by the employees. The legislative power possessed by parliament to permit or require a day to be observed as a holiday does not include the power to legislate (pspecting the terms of contracts of employment on that day. Legislation so requiring wages to be paid would relate essentially to property and civil rights in the province, falling exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, and any such legislation passed by parliament would constitute a colourable attempt to invade the provincial field of legislative power.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, June 3, consideration in committee of Bill No. 21, to amend the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933-Mr. Howe-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

On section 2-Definition of trustees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OP DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the section is agreed to may I say that I was not in the house when it was previously discussed, due to the fact that I was serving on a committee. My reason for rising to-day is to answer some of the criticisms and statements made by hon. members to the effect that it is the intention of the Liberal party through the present measure to come back to a system of political patronage. Many hon. members who spoke yesterday, including the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) viewed with alarm the bill now before the committee, and I felt I could not allow some of the statements to pass which left the impression that the Liberal party was allied with the Canadian National Railways so far as patronage is concerned. Nothing has been said about the other railway in Canada. Nothing has been said about the political patronage exercised by the Canadian Pacific Railway among hon. members of this chamber. As a matter of fact, for many years pressure has been brought to bear by the Canadian Pacific Railway upon hon. members. Even as late as this year it might interest the committee to know that that railway company were much interested in the personnel of the special railway committee which was to be set up.
I am going to mention one instance of political patronage exercised by that railway company among members of parliament. When I introduced my freight rates bill in 1932 I was approached by a high official of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company who, if I interpreted his remarks rightly, threatened me with political death if I dared to proceed with my bill. He pointed out to me what a large concern he represented, and indicated that if I proceeded with my bill I was going to make an enemy for life of this great company. It is just about time the country was .made aware of the outside pressure brought to bear upon members of parliament by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and it might be of interest to find out how many friends of that railway have been approached in the House of Commons. After listening to speeches which were intended to leave the impression that the Liberal party and the Canadian National Railways are close together in matters of patronage, I felt it was about time someone spoke about the other angle of the matter. I am of the opinion that of the two methods, shall I say, which seem to be in existence, the one under which the Canadian Pacific Railway approaches the


Board, oj Directors
members of this house is far more serious and dangerous than that under which any member of parliament approaches any official of the Canadian National Railways.
But the chief reason I rise, Mr. Chairman, is not altogther on that account. I have a suggestion to make which I think would be helpful in the solution of this great railway problem, and it is one which has not been touched on either in this debate or in any other debate in this house to which I have listened.
Every member of parliament is aware of the heavy load which the country is carrying and the heavy interest charges which have to be met each year on the Canadian National Railways, and in all our deliberations with a view to finding a solution of the problem, no one seems to have put his finger on the one spot which, if properly taken care of, might lead to a betterment of conditions and the bringing of our railways up to date. I speak of the labour element. Every attempt that has been made by either of the railways to amalgamate services has brought numerous telegrams and representations from every labour organization in the country, and rightly so, because they fear the dismissal of the rail-waymen. If more serious note were taken of this labour aspect ,of the question, and an investigation made into it as was done in the United States, where there is provision in all their railway mergers for compensating by way of pension the employees dismissed, if we similarly made provision or set up a commission to take care of the men dismissed in any amalgamation or merger of the railways, I believe we might find a solution of this great railway problem. But that aspect of the situation has never been touched. It is true the financial aspect looms largest in the minds of most hon. members. Nevertheless, every time we approach this problem we are met with the question: What shall we do with the men who are dismissed? I am strongly of the opinion that if we set up a commission to look into the possibility of taking care of the men so displaced, we might bring about a solution of Our railway situation. I know that this question has been gone into in the United States and some such plan is afoot there.
Many changes could, of course, be made. In my opinion our whole railway system would have to be brought up to date and modernized. Also there is a lot of material, shall I say, sitting in the various offices of the railways which should be overhauled. Let me give only one instance to illustrate what takes place when a change is made to bring about a betterment in some part of our railway system. In 1934 we noticed as we travelled on
the trains that there was introduced on the menu of the railway dining cars a fifty cent meal at noon and a seventy-five cent or one dollar meal in the evening, but coming to Ottawa this year I noticed that the dining car had reverted to the old charges. On making inquiries I received this explanation as to why they went back to the old prices, and I mention it as an illustration of what takes place when any move is made to bring about betterment in some part of the system. They said that the office staff in Winnipeg objected very strongly to the great number who were dining in the dining car, they were more interested in making two or three hundred per cent profit, irrespective of how small was the number of meals served, than in having a large number of people frequent the dining cars. One could mention dozens of instances of this kind. So long as there are men in the railway offices who are simply dealing with cold figures, so long shall we be disappointed in our efforts to grapple successfully with this railway problem.
To summarize, Mr. Chairman, the two chief points I want to emphasize are: first, the point I made regarding political interference, not in respect of the Canadian National Railways alone, but in regard also to the Canadian Pacific, which occupies a dominant position and takes an active interest in political affairs in this country; and, second, I offer as a contribution toward the solution of the problem the suggestion that we endeavour to devise some scheme of taking care of railway labour that is displaced in any merger. If that question were gone into and some satisfactory arrangement made, as I believe could be done, I think it would lead to placing our railways in a far better position.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OP DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: What is the number of the clause we are considering, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OP DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Clause 2-definition of trustees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OP DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
This is the clause which repeals the section of the old act which provides for the appointment of trustees, and it is the clause upon which I think one may appropriately make general observations with regard1 to the bill.
I believe that this measure and the bill dealing with the Bank of Canada Act are the two most important pieces of legislation which have come before the house this session. They are both significant and undoubtedly will be most important and, I think, vital in their ultimate effects. It is generally recognized that the railway problem is a vital one, and that we ought to give to the railway situation the fullest and most exhaustive
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

study. Inasmuch as this bill is the only measure before parliament, so far as I can recall, under which one can do so, I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to discuss the question briefly.
Does this bill, providing for the abolition of the system of operation under trustees and reverting to the system of operation by a board of directors, offer an adequate or reasonable solution of the railway problem of Canada? I fear, sir, we have to answer that it does not; in fact I cannot help feeling that it may prove to be a boomerang. In saying this I do not wish to give the impression that I am trying to belittle the bill, but I do think it has in it all the elements of, shall I say, an effect adverse to that which it is expected the bill will bring about.
Studying the situation as far as I have been able to do so, I believe that the trustees have given to this country reasonably good service. We cannot expect them, being human beings, to accomplish superhuman results. This railway system is * huge undertaking. I wonder sometimes whether we appreciate the tremendous magnitude of this railway system, not only its importance in the congested centres of the two great industrial provinces of eastern Canada but its extension to the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts, constituting a railway system that I venture to say is perhaps the greatest in the world to-day. In mileage it almost equals the total of Russia's railway system, although Russia has extended her railways in the last few years; but certainly it equals Russia's railway mileage of a few years ago. It is a tremendous system, and to expect that a new method of management, that which was proposed in 1933 for the appointment of trustees, could show the maximum of results by this time is, I think, asking more than could possibly be expected. But I think it advisable to impress upon the committee this fact: According to the reports, as I study them, reasonable results have been achieved under the most difficult circumstances.
Another point I wish to emphasize is that I do not believe the principle of the original act, namely that of providing every means of cooperation between the two great systems, has had a fair trial. In the first place, I do not think there has been time for a fair trial, and in the second place a systematic attack has been made upon the Canadian National Railways throughout the country during the last four or five years, which unquestionably has been a serious handicap to the management of the road. I do not believe parliament can ignoore that fact. That there has
[Mr. Stevens. 1
been, first, a very serious depressed condition, and, second, a continuous attack from the outside to which the railway as a publicly owned body have had little opportunity or no liberty to reply, has constituted a handicap which is unreasonable and unfair. As a result of that, or perhaps I should say in spite of it, the measure of progress achieved by the trustees deserves commendation rather than condemnation.
If I understand the views of the minister who introduced the bill, he contends that the system of trustee management is such that there cannot be achieved the maximum of efficiency. The matter is referred to in the speech from the throne in these terms:
You will be asked to consider amendments to existing legislation respecting the Canadian National Railways, which will serve to afford a greater measure of governmental authority and responsibility to parliament.
Those are broad and general terms which mean little to those not acquainted with parliamentary language. But to me they are an insinuation or suggestion that there has been a lack of a sense of responsibility to parliament during the time the trustees have been in charge, and it is suggested that a reversion to a board of directors form of control will result in a larger measure of sense of responsibility to parliament and a larger measure of control by parliament over the road. That is a distinct challenge to parliament. It is a definite charge against the system of trustee management. I do not think the facts as disclosed in the annual report of the railway as laid before the committee of parliament on Canadian National Railways and Canadian National shipping will justify any such charge.
I feel it would have been better had this bill been left with the committee, dealt with there and returned to the house with the report of the committee, not only upon the bill itself but upon the report of the railway, which is studied in that committee from year to year. Since that has not been done, all we can do is apply to the study of this bill the information which was disclosed in the hearings of the committee dealing with the management of the road. I have not been a member of that committee for some years, although I was a member some time ago, but I have attended some of its meetings and have read some of the evidence given before it. I am convinced that in the examination by the committee of the officers of the Canadian National Railways or in the report of the Canadian National Railways there is no justification for the charge, the statement, or the allegation, what-

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
ever you choose to call it, that the system of management under a board of trustees has been lacking in efficiency or in a sense of responsibility to parliament. That being my conviction, I find it extremely difficult to agree to the cancellation of that system, which is the purpose of the section immediately before us. I regret to place myself in the position of differing from the Minister of Railways, but I cannot help that.
_ The argument that government ownership is always inefficient has been made so often during the last few years that the public has subconsciously absorbed that conviction. We hear this argument everywhere. I saw it in an editorial in one of the leading dailies only a day or two ago-government ownership is in its essence inefficient. A casual comparison of the results of government ownership with the results of private ownership, as -disclosed by the difficulties of the last six years, will, I think, persuade anyone that while government ownership may be attended by certain inefficiencies, private ownership is not free from similar inefficiencies. How often do we see a reference to that great hole in the centre of the city of Montreal as indicating the inefficiency of this road. I was in Montreal the other day and I walked across the viaduct. I must confess it shocks one to see that ghastly excavation which was to be the site of the foundation of a great terminal structure. However, as I stood there I looked to my left and I saw a magnificent building which at a cost of some 820,000,000 to $25,000,000 was erected by one of the most efficient financial organizations in this country. This great organization undoubtedly has men of the highest ability managing its affairs, yet will any one say that that great structure, which is only partly occupied, was a wise expenditure of that concern's money? The two stand there side by side. One is the evidence of perhaps too great optimism on the part of those who headed the national railways a few years ago, while the other is evidence of the superoptimism of private enterprise.
If we are going to compare the efficiency of government ownership with that of private ow-nership, we must go right down the line. For instance, it is said that we are overbuilt in railways in Canada. So we are. There is no use in attempting to disguise that fact; we might as well meet it frankly. The railways have been built; they are here; yet I notice that the great competitor of this national road is attempting to get into the mining areas north of the National Transcontinental line. No one can deny that we have been greatly worried during the last twenty years because of the building of the Transcontinental. That line has been the occasion of rebuke to those who originated it, but it has since been found that it opened up one of the richest mining areas in the world. During the last few years, perhaps more this year than any other, we have begun to realize the value of this area as a source of wealth for Canada. A railroad which is now government owned opened up that area, but there is keen competition on the part of the other railway, which is under private ownership, to go in there to tap some of these rich areas. I am not for a moment discussing the claims of the two-that comes under another bill-but I am pointing out that while for many years the Transcontinental was looked upon as an example of colossal folly in government projection of railway construction, we are now coming to realize that it did open up vast riches in this country.
And so one might go on with many other illustrations. For instance, it is said that the Canadian National has paralleled the Canadian Pacific. Well, if that is true it is also true that the Canadian Pacific paralleled the Canadian National, or the old Grand Trunk in Ontario and the Grand Trunk Pacific on the prairies. So that both systems have perhaps equal responsibility in the matter of overconstruction, but the tendency is always to put the blame on the Canadian National or the government owned system. I think it is wise for parliament to pause and weigh carefully the measure of responsibility. Though that may be now an unprofitable use of time, nevertheless it is advisable to do it if we are to have a proper idea of the responsibility of the government owned system as against the privately owned railway. I will not pursue the comparison further, but I do suggest that it is worthy of very close scrutiny and examination.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) a moment ago referred to the question of the rights of employees, and I wish to supplement his observations by emphasizing the fact that the employees of this great system certainly have rights. And those rights were recognized by the chairman of the system in his address to the committee the other day. I should like to read two brief extracts from that address. I do so because I think the whole statement should be carefully considered, but these particular extracts are applicable to the rights of employees and will serve to bring them home more definitely than any language of mine could. In this statement Judge Fullerton says:
When we took office, admittedly the morale of the men was low. They had seen their numbers reduced from 111,383 to 70,625 and
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

their total compensation reduced from $176,000,000 to $95,000,000. Those whose seniority had so far protected them were uncertain as to the future, their opportunities for promotion slight and their chances of demotion real. They were fearful of proposals for amalgamation and unification, both of which in their view meant disturbance, less work and less pay. I consider it essential in the interests of the railway itself that the conditions of service should be such as to offer at least as much security of employment as do other professions and occupations.
I pause here to emphasize that principle which Mr. Justice Fullerton in his statement has laid down-that the men are entitled to a sense of security in employment. And by the way, this parliament is charged with responsibility not only for the reducing of deficits but for preserving in equity the welfare of its citizens; and in this instance the welfare of these men, their livelihood, their very existence is in our custody in a very direct way. Mr. Fullerton goes on to say:
It seems to have been overlooked that the joint advantage can be secured only by transferring the burden to labour.
I would emphasize that point. That, sir, is one of the principal grievances of workingmen in this and other countries, that as efficiency advances in mechanical development and in other ways, the full burden or almost the full burden of loss is borne by labour. That is inequitable; it is an unfair situation. It is one of the things that civilized countries must face, and we ought to face it in connection with this bill and in connection with the proposals now before us. He says further:
A more equitable arrangement with labour appears to be required and should be provided. If this were done, one great preliminary step towards the accomplishment of any radical changes which might displace labour would be made.
And later on he makes a definite suggestion which I commend to the government and to this committee:
An agreement has been reached between the railway executives and organized labour in the United States providing for the payment of a measure of compensation to employees thrown out of work by consolidation of railway facilities, and I understand that the British railways also made some provision for employees displaced as a result of the amalgamation of British railways into four systems. I have reached the conclusion that the government, the railways and the representatives of railway labour should discuss this matter together with a view to the adoption of some arrangement for the two Canadian railroads as will afford reasonable protection against hardship on the part of those employees who may be displaced by the adoption of cooperative measures.
I listened to Judge Fullerton as he read his statement to the committee, and no one

could help being impressed with the serious nature of this problem as he viewed it. I think that this house ought to pause in the passing of this measure and in the consideration of this whole question so as to ensure that, whatever steps are taken, this phase of the subject will be adequately safeguarded.
Another question impresses itself on my mind. Behind this bill, behind all the discussion, there looms constantly the question of unification or amalgamation. I do not think parliament can disregard it. It might be argued that I am trespassing at the moment upon the rules of the house in introducing that question; but we must not lose sight of the fact that, in the clause immediately before us, we are repealing the section that provides for the present system of management by trustees. That system was inaugurated in this country for the purpose of bringing about ultimately cooperation between the two railways.
One cannot have read the public utterances of persons in high authority on the competing line in recent years without being impressed with this thought-and I am not criticizing Sir Edward Beatty in this matter at all; I think he has a right to his views and it is his duty to those whom he serves to express those views. But we must look at this matter from the standpoint of the welfare, first, of the country as a whole and secondly of the Canadian National system. I have been impressed with this thought, that altogether too much emphasis has been placed by Sir Edward Beatty upon the problem of unification or amalgamation and not sufficient attention has been paid to genuine cooperation with the national system. It may be argued that I am unjust to Sir Edward Beatty in that regard. If I am I regret it, because I hold him in the highest esteem. I repeat that I am not criticizing him for taking any stand he thinks fit to take, but I hold that we as members of parliament should review all sides of the question, and if we differ from him we are bound to give expression to our views. Officials of the Canadian National Railways are prevented from making reply in kind to that sort of argument. For instance, Judge Fullerton or the president of the railway cannot go on the public platform and argue with perfect freedom what he believes to be the best policy; he can speak only guardedly, with reserve and after due consideration of what may be the views of the government-perhaps it would be more correct to say that these officials as such are bound to leave to the government itself declarations of large policy. So they are handicapped, and in the mean-

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
33S1
time there is growing up or being built up in the country a definite body of public opinion which, according to my view, is unfair to the national railways in that it does less than justice to that great system.
So I raise the question of unification and amalgamation, and I ask, is it the only solution? It is cited by many as the only solution of the problem. I do not think it is. Parliament and the people dare not forget that in the Canadian National railway system we have a magnificent asset, and one of stupendous value. True, there are losses. True, we have had every year a cash deficit. But look out over the world, and particularly over the United States; what railway over there but has a deficit? What systems over there, some of them operating in the most densely populated districts of the country, but have received aid from the federal government in the last few years? So, Mr. Chairman, I think above all things we should fix in our minds the fact that we have in this railway a magnificent asset.
The second thing I want to suggest is-and this is a definitely business suggestion-that one should never surrender an asset at the bottom of the market. There has never been a time in the last fifteen years when it was less advisable than it is now to consider any suggestion for the disposal of this system, unless it was in 1933, when things were a little worse than they are to-day. This is no time to tolerate propaganda of any kind for the disposal of what is known as the Canadian National Railways, the property of the people of this country. I am assuming for the sake of my argument and as a reflection of my own views that we ought not to consider unification,-a term, of course, so broad that you can attach to it almost any meaning you like, though I choose to give it the meaning that I think most people do, that it is merely the modern rendition of "amalgamation."
If there is not to be amalgamation or unification, and in my opinion there should not be at this time, what other things can we do, and does this bill offer any new way of dealing with the problem? In the first place I believe, as I indicated at the opening of my remarks, that this bill will be a retrograde step, because under the trustee system of management it would have been easier than it will be under a board of directors to put into effect some suggestions I am about to make.
Here are some things we can do. I admit none of them are new, and I do not pretend to bring under review all the proposals that one might make. There is the matter of the modernization of the service. I have in my
hand an extract from the Wall Street Journal of May 23, 1936. It is headed: Pennsylvania Railroad Speeds Freight Deliveries, and I would ask the committee to give heed to it, because, in my opinion, if more time were spent in studying practical solutions instead of reaching out for the moon we should make much better progress towards the settlement of our railway problem. The article states:
Simultaneously with the inauguration on Monday of system-wide store door pick-up and delivery of less than carload freight at regular station to station rates, the Pennsylvania railroad will extend the range of its overnight merchandise freight deliveries to include hauls of 400 miles and, in many cases, still greater distances. In numerous instances, second morning delivery will be advanced to first morning, reducing the time in transit by a full day. Later and more convenient closing hours for the acceptance of shipments will also be instituted at many points.
That is a statement of what the Pennsylvania Railway is doing in this one rather limited sphere. That road is recognized as one of the most efficient railways and perhaps one of the wealthiest organizations of its kind on the continent. It is progressive and up to date; perhaps more than any other system in the United States it is giving leadership in the modernizing of methods of handling not only freight but passengers and other traffic. But what does this mean? We have had constant complaints during the last ten years about the competition of trucks; it is a real competition and one that is very difficult to meet-. The Pennsylvania railroad, I believe, has met that competition. In part, but only in part, the Canadian railways are doing the same thing. A system-wide store door pick-up: that is one thing. Going right to the place of origin of the freight, picking it up, taking it to the railway, transmitting it by fast freight to the point of delivery and delivering it to the door of the person or the firm to whom it is consigned: that is one element of the Pennsylvania system. The second point is that they give a fast and assured delivery. If Canadian railways, particularly in the congested industrial and commercial areas of eastern Canada, would do the same, they would render a great service to their systems and in large measure would meet the competition of the trucks. The last point is that although this railroad h-as already given a very generous time allowance for the delivery of freight, it has extended that allowance by careful study and good executive management. I cite this merely as an illustration of what is practicable. It is being done; it is nothing new; and certainly it is something that could be followed
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

in this country with substantial advantage to the railway.
The next point has to do with passenger rates. Within the last two years or more, and particularly within the last twelve months, it has become the practice of the two Canadian railways to give cheap passenger excursion rates. I think that could well be extended. I am not prepared to go into details of schedules and passenger rates, but only yesterday my attention was brought to the fact that the cost of travelling to Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto from some intermediate points is such that it would really be a large outlay to the average citizen, particularly in the small towns and rural districts. And the trains are running nearly empty. Stand on the driveway any morning-as I often do, because I make it a habit to walk along about the time these trains go out

and what do you see? A great engine capable of hauling fourteen or fifteen cars, pulling out with only four or five-a baggage and express car, a mail car, a coach or two and a chair car. You can watch the trains go by day after day, month after month and year after year, and you see in them just a handful of people; yet it costs as much to haul that train empty as full. A real and definite lowering of passenger rates would fill up those trains. I wonder whether it ever occurred to the railways that if this were done the movement of package freight might be definitely stimulated, because if people move about by hundreds and thousands it leads to a certain amount of purchasing, which means a larger movement of freight. These are little things, perhaps, but they would contribute to the solution of the problem. I suggest they could be considered with profit.
Then there is the question of carload lots in freight. The present limits are in my estimation altogether too high. Again I am not going to produce data and statistics, but I assert definitely that the minimum car lot is generally speaking too high. Go to any freight yard and watch the loading of the cars; you see a great freight ear with a tare of 36,000 or 37,000 pounds and you see loaded into that car five or ten tons of freight. Dozens of cars go out only partly loaded; or, if they are held to complete the load, the freight that is put in in small lots is delayed and delivery is slow compared with the fast delivery I mentioned a moment ago. Why is it not possible and desirable for the railways to agree to a ten ton minimum carload, thus assuring rapid movement of that freight?
Another thing that should be studied is the whole question, of railway equipment. I have watched these cars for forty years; the only difference between the freight car of to-day and that of forty years ago is that

the car of to-day has a capacity of fifty tons, or sometimes more, whereas thirty or forty years ago I fancy the capacity was twenty or twenty-five tons. It means heavier, costlier, more imposing equipment, but certainly it has not brought about a larger net freight result.
Turning to passenger equipment, we know what has happened in Europe and in the United States in the last two or three years. Railway engineering experts the world over declare that the error of the last two decades has 'been that railway equipment ran to weight, whereas science called for a lessening of weight. Now they are addressing themselves to the task. Here again is a subject which might well receive the attention of the two great railway systems. A complete renovation of railway equipment would probably take ten years and might well be started now; it would give a large amount of employment. Cost-yes; it would cost a good deal, but in net results in the long run it would pay.
All these things could be done, and many others that I have not time to mention, without any conflict of opinion between the roads. It is not a question of amalgamation and unification. Cooperation in the elimination of competing services is sound provided that those who are displaced are reasonably well cared for. But these other matters would increase the efficiency of the roads, would not reduce employment at all, in fact would lead to an increase of employment. In the long run they would tend to increase the returns to and the efficiency of the roads, and they are not subjects which could possibly be looked upon as controversial as between the two railways.
This bill touches only the form or type of management; it does not offer any solution of the railway problem. I think the whole matter could be summed up with this observation; what the railways need is traffic, and what will create traffic? You cannot have traffic if people cannot buy, and people cannot buy goods if they have not purchasing power. That is why I couple this bill with the Bank of Canada Act amendment, because both measures lead us to a consideration of the same subject, namely, the fundamental economic problem of an equitable adjustment of our economic structure so that there may be a larger measure of purchasing power in the hands of the great body of people. Some have expressed it in this way: that out of the consumer's dollar a larger portion may go to the primary producers, who after all outnumber by long odds the rest of the popula-


Board oj Directors
tioa. If their purchasing power could be raised-and I believe it can be-increased traffic would result and the railway problem would be solved.
I conclude by saying, regretfully, that I see no forward step in this proposal. Indeed, as I said at the outset, the repeal of section 3 of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act of 1933, which is the section that inaugurated the system of trustee management, is a retrograde step.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OP DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
With *the latter part of the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay Bast (Mr. Stevens) I am in complete agreement. The railway problem, I need not say, is one of our major problems if not the outstanding problem with which parliament has to deal, and as such it should receive major consideration from the government. The present bill is not such as to lead me to believe that the problem has received major consideration. I need not delve into the history of our railways; that history has been placed on Hansard many times and is there for all to read. I should like to emphasize, however, this fact, that it is a problem which is far too serious to be treated as a political issue. In an address before the Toronto board of trade the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) suggested that the railway problem, more than any other, threatens our national life, and in a recent editorial the Montreal Daily Star suggested that the Canadian railway problem is as an octopus slowly and surely sapping the lifeblood of our country.
There is no question that the railway problem is a very involved one. The point uppermost in my mind is whether or not it is too seriously involved to be capable of solution by any one political party. I am convinced, and I believe many other hon. members feel the same way, that this is a major problem requiring the united action of all Canadians regardless of political affiliation. When I entered parliament at the beginning of this session I had hoped that a problem such as this would receive consideration regardless of political affiliations, but in that respect I have been disappointed.
I should like to amplify certain observations which have been made with regard to railway employees. I have a deep interest in the human aspect of the problem. We must remember that when we are considering a system of this magnitude, when we are dealing with an industry giving employment in Canada to 119,357 persons, the human element is of great importance. The Canadian National Railways employ 65,712 persons, and when we look at these large figures we have
a clear understanding of the magnitude of the system and how it must affect our population. We must remember that many of the railway employees support families, in certain districts large families. When we suggest innovations and changes we must remember that the human element, the employee, is becoming uneasy and uncertain as to the future. We are causing a certain amount of unrest among the employees not only of the Canadian National but of the Canadian Pacific and of other railway systems in Canada. My view is that whatever change we may make in the national system indirectly affects every system in Canada.
At the present time unemployment exists to a considerable degree. A move in the railway field is likely to increase the number of unemployed unless we give careful consideration to the human element involved in the proposed change. I regret very much that so soon after taking office the government elected last October has seen fit to cause unrest among railway employees, who, I suggest, do not deserve that kind of treatment. In such a short space of time the government could not have given adequate consideration to proposals involving the radical changes indicated in the measure before the committee. I agree with the statement made by Judge Fullerton in the report he presented before the committee on railways and shipping on Tuesday morning. He used these words:
Further I cannot conceive of anything more likely to have an unsettling effect upon those engaged in operating the railways than public argument centered on the system, and that whatever satisfaction one might obtain from such controversies they cannot in the end be of benefit to the railways over which I have been placed.
I charge the government with causing a certain degree of unrest and dissatisfaction among railway employees in Canada. They have not acted fairly towards those men and women, and in centres where the people are dependent upon railway employment there is great disappointment with the attitude the government has taken on this major question.
The statement has been made that we are overdeveloped in the matter of railways. With that statement we must all agree, and I need not quote figures to prove its accuracy. In passing, however, I should like to pay tribute to those great men of the past who have made possible our railway systems. We must not forget that the large mileage we criticize to-day was developed in the past by men of vision, men who conceived what Canada would be in the future. Those men deserve our tribute, not our criticism. They builded better than they knew.
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

I look at the railway system as it is centred around Montreal and I think of the tunnel constructed many years ago through Mount Royal. This afternoon there has been reference to a hole in the ground, which is a recent development of the tunnel. Was it as a result of an accident that the tunnel happened to come into Montreal through Mount Royal at the same level as the tracks going into Bonaventure station and over the Victoria bridge? No, it was not. The man who conceived the idea of building a tunnel and approaching the centre of Montreal from the north also appreciated the level of the Victoria bridge and Bonaventure station. He had a vision of the possible development of railway facilities on the island of Montreal, with the result that in the centre of Montreal we have an approach that can be used by any or all railways coming into that city. No, it was not any happy accident that took place in connection with the building of the tunnel. Like all railway developments in Canada, it . was the result of broad vision on the part of the men who conceived it.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has made slighting references to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I hold no brief for that company, but I do not believe they deserve the harsh criticism to which they have been so unfairly subjected this afternoon. That railway has made the Dominion of Canada possible as a nation. Why should we criticize it as it was criticized this afternoon? It has made a great contribution to our national development and should not be subjected to unfair treatment. The hon. member for New Westminster was not fair in his observations. I do not believe Sir Edward Beatty or any of his officials would connive at an act such as was suggested this afternoon. I do not agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) in the suggestion that unification is but another application of the term amalgamation. It is not so. Unification is an altogether different term from amalgamation. My friend from one of the western constituencies invited a definition of unification and amalgamation. I gave him a definition of the term, and I thought I had made my definition quite clear and distinct.
I always try 'to do that, but evidently I failed, or else his failure to comprehend a clear-cut definition fell short of my anticipations. The next morning I was greeted with the suggestion that he appreciated my definition for he would find it of tremendous value to him when he sought reelection in his district the next time an election was held.

I deprecate, Mr. Chairman, lowering the discussion of such an important problem as this to the level of the election possibilities of one or two members of the house.
I have suggested that we have been overdeveloped in our railways, and I could quote figures in support of that. We have in this country a population of 225 per mile of railway, and in the United States the figure is 500 per mile. It is my opinion that our railways will never reach a state of efficiency until our population reaches approximately 25,000,000.
In the railway and shipping committee we discussed railway costs and the losses sustained by the Canadian National Railways. It was my intention to place certain figures on Hansard this afternoon, but I shall refrain from doing so. Anything I say in connection with the Canadian National Railways I do not say in order to knock or in any way to lower the prestige of that railway, because I am just as much convinced as is the hon. member for Kootenay East that the Canadian National Railways has an important part to play in our national development, and as such, as the railway in which we are vitally interested, it should have fair and reasonable consideration. Any figures I give which might be to the detriment of that railway I give only to show that the low figures that obtained under the board of directors prior to 1933 have been improved since the board of trustees came into office.
Previous to 1933 we had a board of directors, very similar to the board of directors now proposed by the government. When the board of directors was in office previously, we recognized the fact that they were struggling against tremendous difficulties, that deficits were increasing to such an extent that they became alarming. The situation was such that on July 16, 1931 the standing committee on railways and shipping passed the following resolution:
Your committee desire to call the attention of the house to the proposal made by Sir Henry Thornton at one of the sessions of the committee. He referred to the serious position of the transportation business generally and recommended that a commission be appointed for the purpose of considering the whole question of Canadian transportation.
That suggestion was adopted, with the result that the Duff commission was appointed. We have heard a great deal about the Duff commission. I just wish that every member of the house was as familiar with that commission's report as I have tried to make myself during the past few weeks. It is a concise statement of conditions as the commission

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
found them during the course of their investigation. Prior to 1933 there had been a board of directors, and the commission was critical of that system of operating the railway. This is what they had to say in connection with the operation of the Canadian National Railways under a board of directors similar to the board of directors advocated at this time by the present government. In paragraph 33, page 13, we find these words:
Running through its administrative practices, however, has been the red thread of extravagance. The disciplinary check upon undue expenditure, inherent in private corporations because of their limited financial resources, has not been in evidence. Requisitions of the management have been endorsed by governments, and successive parliaments have voted money freely, if not lavishly.
Again, in paragraph 34, on the same page, we find these words:
Within the railway organization there has been freedom in expenditure and encouragement in plans for expansion and extension of services which were inconsistent with prudent administrative practices. The administration failed to realize that this country, with the greatest railway mileage in the world in relation to population, could not afford further capital and maintenance expenditures for unwarranted branch lines, for de luxe services, for uurequired hotels, for the building of ships in competitive service to be shortly abandoned; and, generally, for costly adventures in competitive railways out of proportion to the needs of the country.
Again, in paragraph 142, the Duff report goes on to say:
The conduct of the affairs of the national railway has been subjected in the past to political and public pressure.
Again, in paragraph 145:
Under the circumstances, the directors' functions have been in practice nothing more than advisory. It would seem that they generally gave formal approval to programs of expenditures which they appeared to regard as the main concern of the president and the government. This left the railway open to political influence and to public pressure exerted by communities and by associations of business and labour interests.
Again, in paragraph 146:
Of direct political interference by ministers and members of parliament in the detail operations of the railway, we were assured by the officials there was little or none. It was in the larger sphere of policy that political considerations led to unwise and unnecessary capital expenditures, the result of which was to create an atmosphere in which the ordinary principles of commercial operation of the railway were lost sight of.
There was the condition brought out in the Duff report. That report, which was produced at great cost to the country, and tabled in the house, represented the consensus of 12739-210
able men appointed to study a particular problem, and to-day despite that report, despite its recommendations, the government proposes to go back to the very things that were strongly condemned in that report. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, and through you the other members of this committee: is it fair to the people of Canada to institute a commission of that kind, with all the expenses involved, and then disregard its report? Is it any wonder that Judge Fullerton, emphasizing these particular things, uses these words:
These rvere the fundamental defects which the Duff commission believed could be remedied by a trustee system of direction. I wish to say most emphatically that we have exerted every effort to vindicate the hopes of the commission, and to add with some pride that, having regard to the brief time so far elapsed, we have achieved a substantial measure of success. So far as I have ever heard, there has not even been an allegation that the board of trustees has been influenced in the slightest degree by any political consideration at any time. The board has acted at all times, or endeavoured to act, as business men of broad and far-reaching responsibilities would act.
That is his opinion after two and one-half years experience as chairman of the board of trustees. Despite that experience, despite his considered opinion and despite the Duff report, we have before us a measure which will revert back to the conditions prevailing prior to 1933. I do not think it is fair to parliament or to the people to ask for consideration of a measure such as this. In his remarks yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggested that the government had a mandate from the people, but the people gave no mandate to disregard a report for which they paid a considerable amount of money, a report based on considered information and supported by subsequent events. I do not think the government has any right to suggest that the people have had the opportunity to pass on legislation of this kind.
In my opinion this bill will restore political influence in connection with the management of the Canadian National system. There is every evidence of the possibility of government interference and political control. I have only to refer to the remarks of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe) during the course of a speech delivered in Toronto, not months after his taking office, not a year after, but just a few weeks. The Toronto Daily Star of December 9, 1935, gives his considered opinion on this question of major importance. He said:
The 1933 legislation which abolished the board of directors and substituted the trustee form of direction removed control of this directing agency from the hands of the gov-
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

eminent and placed it in the hands of parliament, the Commons and the Senate, though the latter might not he in any sense representative of public opinion as expressed in the election of the representative chamber. It went further. The act provided that the person with the titular rank of president shall report and be responsible to the trustees and them alone. Thus the government representing the owners, has, under the present legislation, no control whatever.
That is the statement of the minister, made less than two months after taking office. He was going to abolish the present system and take control to himself or to his department. He seeks to get the direction of the Canadian National Railways. He assumes that that direction has been lost. One of the presumptions of the Duff report was that it had been lost to political influence, and the minister now seeks to bring it back under that political influence. It was established by witnesses who appeared before the Duff commission that it was detrimental to the railway to be under political influence, and yet the Minister of Railways has introduced legislation to bring that very condition back into the system. I have talked to railway employees and they deprecate such a move. They are entirely opposed to anything that savours of political influence in connection with the operation of the Canadian National Railways. I hope the minister will take cognizance of their objections and of the other objections which have no doubt been voiced throughout the country. The minister continued:
The purpose of the trustee form of management was to take the railway act out of politics. I wish this were possible. As Minister of Railways, I have no desire to interfere with the expert management of the road. My concern is the reverse, which is interference by the railroad management with the expressed policies of the government. We cannot escape the fact that the railway is owned by the people of Canada, that taxes collected from the people pay its deficits and that the prosperity of every citizen in thousands of communities from coast to coast can be affected by its managerial policies. Mine is a railroad riding-[DOT]

speechtext: The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Howe) has denied that he said what the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) quoted him as saying. The hon. member would be out of order in continuing to refer to that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the matter is closed.
Anything I have said that casts any reflection upon the minister, I happily withdraw, because I would not like to do anything of that sort.
The hon. member is referring to what somebody other than the minister said, and he has a right to do that.

I was referring to the situation that existed prior to 1933. This situation which was recognized by everyone had been brought about through the operation of the Canadian National Railways by a board of directors. It could be clearly inferred from the Duff report that that method of management had given rise to a considerable amount

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
of political interference in connection with the operation of the railway. The point I am trying to make is that all this was done away with by the board of trustees. We now have a measure to reestablish that influence in connection with our Canadian National system.
I commenced by suggesting that this was a major problem, one that was beyond the ability of any one party to solve. I feel that that is so. This problem should be over and above all political parties. As one newspaper suggests, if we do not solve it, chaos will result. I urge the solution from that point of view. What the government has brought down is no solution; it will never alleviate the distress caused by the deficits that are piling up at the present time. This year we have $115,000,000 to pay out of our treasury in connection with the Canadian National Railways. How much longer can this country continue to pay amounts equal to that without going under? I leave it to the imagination of hon. members. How much longer can the people of Canada supply through taxes the deficits that are being piled up by the Canadian National Railways? I say again, as I said before, that anything that affects the Canadian National Railways indirectly affects our other great railway system, the Canadian Pacific. I wish therefore to urge the considered opinion of this house with respect to this question, an unbiased opinion. I want to see the question raised above the political issue. I should prefer to see the minister strike out this clause and continue with the board of trustees, who have been in office only since December, 1933. They have been in office just long enough to get the idea of what a railway is, and they are producing results; the reports this year show that the system is improving. If that is so-and we assume it is, according to the reports before us-why change something that is improving a bad condition? Why not continue the board in office for a certain period in order to give the trustees an opportunity to work out their policy? Raise it above political party.
The other evening I read an article from which I should like to quote:
But what have we done at the instance of this government to solve the problem involved in the net loss of $115,000,000 in the railways last year?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will be good enough to state what the article is from which he is quoting.

With all due

The hon. member was not quoting from anything said by any person outside this house, nor was he commenting upon or [DOT] criticizing anything done in the house. I suggest that it would be necessary to invoke some other rule; but I may add to what my leader has said in that regard, with respect to the rule about not quoting from articles, that it has been more honoured in the breach than in the observance.

On the question of order, Mr. Chairman, I would point out that what you have just read is paragraph 306 of Beauchesne's volume, and it is not a rule. Some years ago we made the mistake, in quoting from Beauchesne, of citing paragraphs

The rules of this house are the standing rules of the house, and parliamentary practice is the practice that has developed under the rules; and Mr. Beauchesne, in this admirable book, quotes Bourinot at page 336 as authority for his summary or precis of the law. Unfortunately however it is not a rule; it is simply a summary of Bourinot's book at page 336. You will recall the time at which that error was made; it was in connection with the question whether or not a member was bound to vote if he remained in the house. Reference was made to what was called a rule but it turned out to be a paragraph not founded upon a rule. It is easy to see why it was referred to as a rule-I think I did myself refer to it at that particular time as a rule, but my attention was directed to the fact that it was not. I do wish we had a universal rule with respect to the reading of newspaper articles, because there are 245 members in the house, and when someone else, a 246th member, is quoted because he happens to be a particular person, we are likely to get into great difficulties. I once heard a distinguished jurist, a Lord Chancellor, say, when reference was made to Berriedale-Keith's eminent work, "Who is he?" As a matter of fact, quotations from living authors are usually not used in courts of law. There are one or two great exceptions, Benjamin on Sales, and likewise Buckley on Companies. In the meantime the hon. member has Hansard, so that the difficulty is avoided.
