speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member for Mount Royal, but he has already exceeded his time, and has had credit for the time spent on the point of order.

I am about to finish the
quotation:
They have the majority, they have the power, and I trust they have the inclination. Let them proceed to give effect to their inclination and they will receive the support of those members of the house who are interested in the solution of this problem.
I desire to leave the problem on that high level, the utterance of a statesman who is recognized as such throughout this country, and to ask that the government give the matter consideration in the spirit of that pronouncement.

In speaking on this very important bill, I wish to be hrief, recognizing that we expect to complete in short order the remaining work of the session. At the outset I thank the hon. minister for the manner in which he has brought this matter to the attention of the House of Commons and the country as a whole. Certainly no one on either side of the house can accuse him of partisanship in his method of presentation of the bill; he dealt with it in that businesslike way which befits a matter so important to the people of this dominion, and one in which every citizen is greatly interested. It is not my intention to go over ground that has been covered by previous speakers in the presentation of figures regarding the railways of this country. We all know that our railway systems are very important and very expensive. Nevertheless, in dealing with this subject we must keep an open mind, realizing that when the fathers of confederation and those who pioneered in new inventions fostered the development of our railway transportation services, no one dreamed of the changes that have taken place in these latter years and which have to some extent replaced those services. Even members of parliament may sometimes feel a little astonished at this phase of our progress when dealing with certain of the items of the federal administration, for instance, the Post Office Department. Some now are dreaming of the day when our postal service will in the main be conducted by air. No one will criticize this progress and development, for after all we must be on the march if we are to keep abreast of civilization.
But there is one factor we cannot avoid in discussing railway questions in this country,
namely, that unlike some sections of the United States or some countries on other continents we shall always need railway facilities, at least during certain times of the year. No one will challenge this statement, that no matter what we may do with our trans-Canada highway, which is going to parallel our present railway system from coast to coast, in the winter months we shall require our railway facilities, not only in the northern sections of Canada but in the southern ones as well. In dealing with this matter, therefore, we must apply our minds to this consideration, that no matter how much we deplore the deficits on the Canadian National Railways and the burden that is thereby laid on the shoulders of every taxpayer of this country, we must deal with the question in a way that will not jeopardize the services to which our people are entitled during every month of the year, and more particularly in the winter. If there is one suggestion I would particularly like to commend to the present government, it is that they should appoint a transportation department, with which it may be found possible for the various provinces to be associated, and with only one head of the transportation system we have in this country, so as to have uniform transportation regulations. There is no evading the fact that we are going to have deficits. Everyone will have been struck with the inroads that have been made into railway business by the bus and truck services of this dominion, and those inroads are going to be deeper and deeper unless we find it possible to put the two systems on an even keel, where we shall have uniform legislation and regulations, and where one will compete with the other with an equal chance of success, and with definite fields of action. I fully understand that this is very dangerous ground. No doubt these questions have been mooted at provincial conferences held in Ottawa. I also readily recognize that for sentimental reasons, if for no othei'3, the various provinces wish to have the full say so far as truck and bus services are concerned. But I believe the situation is so serious, and that fact is so fully appreciated by the provinces, that the time will soon be ripe for the creation of a centralized service, a central department that will look at transportation from all angles and will function along the line of definite activities emanating from the central government.
Speakers on behalf of the opposition would have us believe that politics have been injected into the consideration of this problem and this bill, but I believe implicitly in any new measure which will improve, in my opinion, the position of our railways, and I

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
surely hold that the Montreal Star is not being fair to the Canadian National railway system or to Canada as a whole when it deals in a biassed way and with far-fetched criticism with the operations of that system. As has been said by a previous speaker, no one will deny that the Canadian National Railway is a wonderful asset to this country. I admit that in certain features of administration it has sinned, and sinned grievously, but surely we shall take note of the mistakes of the past and thereby benefit in future as far as that great system is concerned.
In this discussion frequent reference has been made to the human factor. That is one which no person can wish to ignore, and it seems to me that in the so-called cooperation upon principles of economy which has been applied for the last five years in the Canadian National system, the little fellow, the working man, the one that sweats and toils, has been neglected in a good many cases in contrast with the treatment which has been enjoyed by higher officials. I do not pretend to be a railway man, but when I see a man working on a section of track getting $2.40 a day, while at the same time some high officials of the system are receiving tens of thousands of dollars a year, I can understand tl i>
agitation which is going on in some sections of the dominion. More than that, when 01 id! sees that only two men are engaged on twelve miles of railway, and have to keep that track in good condition-which I maintain is absolutely impossible-while at the name time high officials of the system are travelling over the country in palatial coaches, enjoying the finest possible sendee, one may have to admit that it is less important that officials should have these luxuries than that better provision of necessities should be extended to the working man. The human factor has received consideration so far as the higher officials are concerned, but the men working on the sections or in the shops have not for the last five years received from the administration of the Canadian National Railways the consideration to which they were entitled. I believe that talent and experience should receive a fair recompense. On the other hand labour men have to work under all climatic conditions; I have known them to work ten consecutive hours in a great downpour of rain and at the end of the day get $2.40, and I say that is not fair and not conducive to the esprit de corps that should mark such an organization. I have taken up the cudgeis for these men in the past and I am going to continue doing so. The minimum wage law should be applied on the Canadian National system. Two section men [Mr. Bradette.l
to twelve miles of main line railway is not sufficient. Some day there may be an accident resulting in heavy loss or grievous bodily harm, and the blame should be put where it properly belongs. I do not want to go into that situation at length, but the Canadian National system should realize the competition they have to meet. I have not yet heard of the president or directors of some bus or truck company having a special bus to travel in over the country. Such companies do not have the administration overhead that prevails in the Canadian National Railways.
There is another factor I wish to mention. Take my own section. A young man doing office work or any railway worrk there has no chance whatever of advancement. It seems to be a kind of family compact; the bigger positions go to men in the bigger centres. Surely, in the smaller places young men of experience, with years of service, should have opportunities of promotion. But this is never the case. I do not want to criticize the appointments that took place in my own section, but local men who know all the conditions should receive consideration. Nevertheless men from Montreal, or Quebec, or Toronto, or Winnipeg were placed over men in our section who had years of service and seniority.
There is one section of the Canadian National Railways which has never received proper attention from any government. I am absolutely at ease in speaking about that matter because I have done so every session for the last ten years. That section is the transcontinental link of the Canadian National Railways. Sir Wilfrid Laurier had the great dream that some day a major portion of passenger and freight traffic would go over that section. Perhaps now, through lack of maintenance, the road-bed is not too good and the service would not compare with some other services, but the fact remains that that section has never received the attention it deserves. According to the Duff report, on more than eight hundred miles of main line of the Canadian National system the commissioners did not find it possible to spend a single hour during their inquiry. Every one knows that progress in Canada at the present time is northward and westward. Anyone who knows the mining history of this country knows that progress is being made mostly in the northern sections, especially of Ontario and Quebec. What happened in 1931? Without our section of the population ever being consulted the daily train service we had from Montreal and Quebec via Cochrane to Winnipeg was cut off. To-day there are

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
400,000 people in that area who have been deprived of direct communication with western Canada. Is this fair? It is not. There is only fifteen miles' difference between the route through my section and the routing at present followed by the Canadian National.
I am practical enough to realize that it would not be fair to ask the same kind of palatial trains that we had prior to 1931. Often I criticized the luxurious equipment they had. But this is a fact in which every hon. member is directly interested, that there are at present 400,000 Canadian people deprived of direct communication with the west. If I want to travel from my own home town to Winnipeg I have to go 255 miles out of my way to North Bay. It is true there are local trains twice a week, but will anyone travel on a mixed train the schedule of which is so uncertain that he may reach Winnipeg in a week or it may be two? One of the main reasons I am speaking here now is to make an appeal to the Minister of Railways and to the House of Commons to give a proper train service to a pioneer section of the country, a section the population of which is increasing at the rate of 5,000 a month, and is going to continue to increase. In my own riding I have at present 100,000 people; it is part of a riding which was one riding fifteen years ago, and which is now divided into four. This shows the unfair treatment we receive from an institution that is supposed to give us service; it forgets the human factor. I have been told by some high officials of the Canadian National Railways that they cannot make time on our section. I know they cannot, but there is a very good reason, namely that they have neglected the roadbed. I said that there are only two section men to twelve miles of railway. I am begging this committee, not only the minister but every hon. member present, to study the situation. I do not believe in deficits, but at the same time this country owes something to its population. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) said that the Canadian National Railways is a wonderful asset. He also mentioned the fact that we are spending tens of millions of dollars for war pensions, and I never heard a word of criticism of that from any section of the house. These are liabilities, contracts, for which the dominion carries a certain responsibility.
It is not my intention to deal with this matter at any greater length now; I hope other opportunities will be given me, either before the department or the management of the Canadian National system, to state my case. I hold that under the new board of
directors for which the minister is making provision it should be possible to decrease interest rates on the Canadian National bonds. No one will challenge the statement that when the people invested in those bonds years ago the situation was different from what it is at the present time. If interest rates were reduced fifty per cent that would practically wipe out the deficit. I hope the minister will look into that question. I know it has been given attention by previous administrations.
As far as I am concerned I never had any quarrel with the Canadian Pacific railway ; everyone realizes the good it has done this country and the great part it has played in its development, but the same principle should apply, as forcibly or more so, to the Canadian National Railways. A previous speaker mentioned the Duff report. We see from that report how many roads were unloaded on the Canadian National system. In a good many cases they were unloaded by provincial governments, and those amalgamations were compulsorily loaded on the Canadian National Railways. We cannot expect the Canadian National system to carry all these roads. I make this fervent plea to the minister. I have confidence in his ability; I say this sincerely and I am seldom inclined to praise, but since he has been minister all the presentations he has made in the house have been made in a businesslike way, and I have implicit faith that he will be successful in eliminating some of the troubles that at present face our railway system.
I have been elected to the federal parliament to help every section of Canada, and we must face problems in a national way. Parochialism has never been and never will be my weakness. When I say that at the present time we have not the passenger accommodation between east and west to which we are entitled, I am speaking not politically, but in a national way. I am not fighting only for my constituents; I am speaking for 400,000 people in northern Ontario and northern Quebec, and voicing the sentiment, I believe, of every hon. member and citizen in Canada. An improvement and the reestablishment of the above passenger service would be beneficial not only to the section in which I am most interested, but to the whole of Canada.

Several yearn ago I was employed as a railway telegrapher. At that time I worked on what was known . as the "7/12/365/40-system, without." That meant seven days a week, twelve hours a day, three hundred and sixty-five days a year and forty
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

dollars a month without vacation. Due to the improved intelligence of railway officials and to an increased realization of the value of railway telegraphers the situation has been improved. To-day they are in a much better position.
Much has been said in connection with the higher points of railway administration. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) referred to the habit of reaching for the moon. I believe that sometimes in the discussion of great and important questions there is a tendency to think of the higher-ups and overlook the ones at the bottom. As the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) stated, the human interest element must enter into the successful operation of a railway company. While that element may seem to be of minor importance, in my view it is of great importance because it may reflect either for or against the standing of a railway company.
May I call the attention of the minister and of the board of railway commissioners, if possible, to the situation existing in connection with a service which is only of minor importance so far as railway administration is concerned, but of greater importance as it affects the public. I refer to the railway depot service given by red caps. Some hon. members may smile; when we refer to people at the bottom it is sometimes easy to smile. I must say, however, that the situation with respect to this particular service does not commend itself to the respect of the public.
Let me illustrate. There are about sixty red caps in the union depot at Toronto, only ten of whom receive wages, and small wages, at that. The other fifty are thrown on to the generosity of the public with the result that a government owned railway is encouraging the vicious system of tipping. In other words these boys-we refer to them as boys, but most of them are young married men, some of whom have families-are forced to make their living by receiving tips from the public. In many cases those young married men are receiving such small amounts of money each day that the city of Toronto through its welfare and relief department must subsidize their receipts so that they may live. It is a sad situation when a government owned railway retains employees who render a first-class service to the public, but at the same time pays so little for that service that the workers have to rely upon municipal assistance. The situation I have described applies in other cities where there are union depots.
There is this further point to be considered: The last speaker mentioned that only two men are used to work a twelve mile section. When I worked for the railway a section was five miles long, and five men worked on it.

I do not know what the situation is in Ontario with respect to the numbers employed on sections, but any person using the sleeping cars between Ottawa and Toronto will readily realize that there are certain spots so rough that one almost needs to be fastened into the berth for fear of rolling out. It is evident that an insufficient number of men are being used to patrol the tracks and to keep them in satisfactory condition.
I have referred to these two human interest points, namely the employment of more men on track work and the placing of red caps on a basis whereby they may live without receiving help from municipalities. The giving of assistance simply places another burden on municipalities already overburdened.

Mr. Chairman, we are discussing section 2 of the bill which has to do with the definition of the term "trustees." This section stands as the basis for the whole bill. I suggest that the act passed in 1933 known as the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act was of a judicial nature, because it was based upon the findings of the Duff commission. Each railway was to appoint an arbitral tribunal, the functions of which were to be judicial. It was never intended that the tribunal should be in politics. The gentlemen who formed the tribunal were to perform certain duties as set forth at page 66 of the Duff report, paragraphs 215, 216, 217, 218 and 219.
Hon. members will notice the provision appearing in paragraph 218 of the Duff report on the functions of this joint tribunal.
There shall be no appeal to any court in Canada from any decision of the arbitral tribunal on any question of law or fact; except as to a question of law' if it is one involving a question of jurisdiction, in which case there should be an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, by leave of a judge of that court.
In the present instance the trustees are to be known as directors; in that regard we are becoming more like the Canadian Pacific Railway every day in our "me too" political policy. We should never have moved the head office of the Canadian National Railways from Toronto to Montreal. I have every respect for the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe). I realize that he is a new minister, but the longer he stays in Ottawa the more he will realize that it is politics, politics, all politics all the time.
. May I say that the three gentlemen who served on the board set up by the act of 1933 rendered a good service, one of them without salary, Mr. F. K. Morrow of Toronto, a brilliant young Canadian. They effected

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
economies, and we have but to look at the railway report and examine the operating ratio set out in the Duff report to realize the good work they have done. They have struck off huge maintenance charges, and I must say that the work of the Bennett board was wonderful and satisfactory. In the present instance we are to substitute for that board of three trustees a board of sevenfold amen board of directors.
The employment commission was selected along political lines, and I must say that that is a step in the wrong direction. The same practice will be followed in the present instance of a sevenfold amen board of directors for three trustees a difference without a distinction. Without any notice in votes and proceedings the minister had a committee appointed, violating every rule of parliament, immediately preceding one of the holidays and without any notice whatever they got away with it. No one knew anything about it. It was not on the order paper; no notice was given. It was the only opportunity we had to discuss this most important question of the national railways, involving such huge deficits that it will be an old man of the sea on the backs of the next generation.
The very object of passing this Bill No. 21 is set out in section 2, which is the gist of the whole bill. All the rest of the clauses are merely subsidiary and are built round section 2. Section 2 deals with the definition of the new trustees, who will be a lot of useless figureheads, and their duties. The duties of the board of trustees which were set out in the statute of 1933 were derived from the Duff commission's report. What were those duties? The board of trustees was to get together regarding the joint, use of terminals; running rights and joint use of tracks; control and prohibition in respect of the construction of new lines, and provision of facilities and additional services; the joint use of facilities where this would promote economy or permit the elimination of duplicating or unremunerative services or facilities; abandonment of lines, services or facilities; pooling of any part or parts of freight or passenger traffic; things necessarily incidental to the above enumerated matters.
The very next clause of the Duff commission's report, which was signed by Right Hon. Chief Justice Duff, sets out the jurisdiction of the board of trustees. There is no appeal to any court of law. The Duff commission's report at pages 50 and 51 gives the reasons for the board's recommendations which were incorporated in the statute of 1933, chapter 33. That whole act was built
on the Duff report. Now we are asked by Bill No. 21 to turn that act of 1933 upside down founded as it was on fact and destroy all the good work that has been done under the administration of the board of trustees during the last three years. The board of three trustees was an economic, useful and nationally efficient judicial body, and it is to be replaced by a board of seven directors of no experience with different functions and political powers, and the railway is to be run from the political and not the economic *aspect. At page 50 of their report the Duff commission gives the operating ratios of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, from which I will quote a few figures, as follows, to show the necessity of running the road outside the small realm of politics from the commercial aspect. This railway will be an old man of the sea on the backs of our poor taxpayers for twenty-five to fifty years. This table shows it:

The Duff commisison gave these reasons above why the new board of trustees which it recommended should be freed from political and public pressure. They called in the presidents of the two railways, Sir Edward Beatty and Sir Henry Thornton, and got their views on this subject, and the commission would not have recommended a board of trustees had it not been for the evidence that was given by the president of the Canadian National Railways and of the Canadian Pacific Railway on political influence and its baneful effects which is cited on page 51 of the Duff report. Sir Henry Thornton said:
The leaders of all political parties and the people of Canada as a whole are a unit in their desire to prevent political invasion of the Canadian National Railway.
That was his very first statement. The report goes on to say that the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway appeared to be more concerned over the activities of what he termed "politically-minded" executives of the publicly owned railway than he was over straight political pressure for definite ends. Sir Edward Beatty said:
We talk a great deal about political interference being damaging to railway operations, and we know that that is true, generally speaking. But when we say it we seem to
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

think the only political influence is that exercised by a government, or a member of government, or a member of parliament. To my mind the worst kind comes from the political attitude of men in publicly-owned institutions. Possibly they are not conscious of it, but they become politically-minded; their policies and actions have a political tinge, and that, from my standpoint, is more serious as representing the attitude of the corporation than the isolated act of a member of parliament who tries to get a man employed.
Years ago the ability of privately-owned railway companies to withstand political pressure was somewhat limited. To-day it is nothing like it was, because we can say no to that kind of pressure. But the politics that develop inside an organization because it is publicly-owned, and not privately-owned, is a serious thing.
We are going to upset all the good work that the board of trustees, appointed in pursuance of the Duff report, has done. Liberal newspapers, such as the Toronto Globe, for instance, are taking a great interest in this question of public ownership. I am for public ownership, but I am not out for the kind of public ownership that we see in the Canadian National Railways. There never was and never will be public ownership in the Canadian National Railways because the present system is but the leavings of a lot of privately owned roads, and it is bankrupting the country. The Toronto Globe takes very strong ground on the method, as proposed in this bill, of selecting the railway directors, and it has a great deal to say in praise of the three trustees who are to be removed for this "sevenfold amen" directorate, and particularly in praise of Mr. F. K. Morrow, for what he has done in eliminating what has been termed this reckless and criminal waste of public funds.
We find that the Drayton-Acworth commission in 1917 made parallel recommendations to those made by the Duff commission, namely, that there should be a joint arbitral tribunal working not from any political aspect but solely from the commercial aspect. In the early days of public ownership in your constituency, Mr. Chairman, this very same issue came up, whether there should be political influence in the public ownership of heat, light and power in the hydro development. The Drayton-Acworth report is founded upon the parallel principle of that hydro system that we find in the Duff commission's report, of a publicly owned utility being operated not from a political standpoint but commercially. That is what the Duff and Drayton commission in 1917 recommended should obtain in connection with the board of trustees that was appointed to operate this public utility. The board of three trustees, from 1933 to 1936,

has not had a chance in the two or three years of its existence to show what it could do, and I am sorry to see this change being made. Mistakes have been made in the past, and they are well known to parliament. Parliament has practically no control over the Canadian National Railways. If you ask the Minister of Railways, a new minister, a question about the Canadian National Railways, he replies that he cannot say anything about it because it is a matter for the railway.
It was always intended that any member of parliament could attend the committee on railways and shipping, and ask questions, but members have not yet received the reports of the committee except Nos. 1 to 6. This Bill No. 21, which is now before us, is nothing but a political bill, and the Canadian National Railways will not have a chance under the board of directors which the bill proposes to appoint. The minister should give some evidence as to whom the government is going to appoint. The newspapers seem to know ahead who the seven directors are going to be. All is politics and the games of the ins and .outs, that is all Bill No. 21 is. We all remember the board which had control under the Liberal administration. We remember the conditions under which officials did not even have to put in vouchers for expenditures. We remember how $350,000 was spent for advertising and editorials in newspapers to boost the president and certain directors. We remember how branch lines were built to the sun, to the moon and to the stars. We remember the Cook's tour of a small standing army of officials that travelled all over Europe. Evidence of this disgraceful expenditure is to be found in the 1932-33, 600-page book of the select committee on railways and shipping, and bills from the different hotels throughout Europe. All this was done at the expense of the people of Canada and these officials were exempted from ever putting in any vouchers for these hundreds of thousands of dollars of corrupt and dishonest expenses as set out in the committee's reports.
Are we going back to the conditions which existed in those days? Are we going to build more golf courses, hotels, useless branch lines, and a thousand other things and have deficits all along the line? Are we going back to the building of branch lines, referred to in the Duff report? We have 44,000 miles of single track railway with a population of only nine or ten millions. Our railway mileage equals that of France, Germany and the United Kingdom, with total populations of 47,000,000, 46,000,000 and 45,000,000. Expenditures on branch lines in Saskatchewan amounted to $30,000,000; in Manitoba the

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
total expenditure was S9,862,000; in British Columbia, $5,210,000, and in Alberta, $8,600,000 These branch lines were constructed over the nead of parliament in an absurd way with useless duplication and waste. All this money was spent by the old board1 whom Bill No. 21 now reestablishes, and the old order is back on us. Whenever we asked for information we were told that we could not get it. The province of Ontario and Quebec, where 80 per cent of our cash revenues come from, got little or nothing under the political management to which the Drayton and Duff reports referred. This is to be found in the Duff report commencing at page 50. That report suggests that a non-political board should be appointed.
The central provinces have to pay the deficits. Only a small percentage of the necessary money will come from the workers in the other provinces. Central Canada has to make up these deficits through income and sales taxes and other taxes of that kind. Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to the rights of the majority, but this is the first time I ever knew of a majority having any rights in Canada. The taxpayers of Ontario and Quebec pay eighty per cent of the taxes. The Prime Minister said that he had a mandate from the people, but he never received a mandate to change the management of this railway. The head office was moved from Toronto to Montreal, and it should be moved back to Toronto, the home of public ownership. The national railways should be given a chance to rid itself of the grafters in its make-up and management and organization. A large residence in the city of Montreal was bought for the former president. These new trustees most likely will come from St. James street too, and I should like to know if new houses will be bought for the new president and his sevenfold amen crew of directors.
These new trustees will have their hands tied under section 2. This section is an antithesis to the recommendations of the Duff report. As I say, I have great respect for the minister. I knew him years ago when he was a very likeable, able and capable civil engineer of good repute. Under this bill, neither he nor any other living man will be able to rid this railway of political influence in its administration, that type of influence which has been a curse since confederation in this country. There will be no freedom under this bill. There is no longer any freedom in this parliament, in the press, the pulpit or the universities in this country. There is no freedom I say in the press in this country as its members refuse to have anything to do with reporting the proceedings of this house except what the government cares to have the union press publish. There is no freedom in the pulpit and there is no freedom in our legislatures. We are going back to where we were before the days of responsible government.
Hundreds of millions of dollars were spent without the authority of parliament. I can remember one time when I wanted certain information from the board of directors and the minister told me that he had nothing to do with the matter. He refused to give me a detailed statement of $400,000 which had been spent on paid editorials in the newspapers of this dominion in an effort to boom the president of the Canadian National Railways. Money was spent over the head of this parliament and when we asked for information, the minister told us that he had nothing to do with the matter. If the hydro, that great public enterprise in the province of Ontario, in which tens of millions of the people's money has been invested, had been conducted in the same way as this railway was conducted, that enterprise would have been bankrupt and the province would have been bankrupt. We are going back to the dark days which existed when I first came into this house.
I give a great deal of credit to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and to that other faithful follower of his, the former lovable member for Muskoka, Mr. McGibbon. The latter is a very sick man to-day, the press say, nearly at death's door, but he did a great national work in connection with this railway as a real public ownership man. The people of Canada owe him a great debt of gratitude for the way in which he explored and disclosed the rotten state of affairs that existed in the administration of this railway under the old board of directors. He performed a duty to the people of this country. The Duff report says that this old board acted only in an advisory capacity. They loafed round their offices in Montreal and did nothing. They appeared before the committees here and they sat up in the galleries while the debates were going on, and smoked cigars. They had a good time all over Canada.
I can remember when I tried to start my national coal supply policy in 1923 and to get this railway to adopt a proper national policy in connection with the carriage of coal from the maritime provinces and the western provinces to central Canada. The former board of trustees were absolutely opposed to this, Sir Henry Thornton said I wanted a lunch counter system of freight rates for coal and steel and iron, yet under a system brought about- by the former government along these
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

lines of my coal bill of 1923 to 1930, over 2,800,000 tons of coal were moved economically last year to central Canada and ;he head of the lakes. This movement has jeen of great benefit to the maritime prov-nces and Alberta. Yet the old political crowo in the Canadian National Railways ridiculed it, although it is law to-day.
The government might as well appoint seven directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway to operate the Canadian National system, :or they know more about the system than members of parliament do and will know all that the new seven under Bill 21 know. When we asked for information from the old board, under the political administration, we could not get it; a. member of parliament could not find out anything about the Canadian National Railways. But the head office of the Canadian Pacific Railway knew everything that was going on. That was proved by evidence given here in 1932 before the railway committee, evidence covering nearly four or five hundred pages in the 1932 report on railways and shipping. Do we want to go back to that state of affairs? Yes, and Bill 21 brings us back to the oldi big I days of 1923 to 1930.
I have ne%*er faltered in my support of public ownership, but we have never had public ownership in the National railways, only a name. The present situation has been advertised all over the United States as an evidence of the failure of public ownership, but as I say we have never had public ownership. If the government want to hand over the whole system to private interests, then they are doing the right thing in appointing seven directors. We are simply imitating the Canadian Pacific in referring to the trustees as directors. These directors, I assume, will have private cars and will travel round the country. King Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like the former president and those under him from 1923-1930. There was never anything like it except in the United States. The sections that constitute the backbone of this bill are political in their implications. In Cleveland they have the headquarters of a four billion dollar railway like this under Mr. Van Sweringein comprising twenty corporations, the whole system having been built up on credit, and we all know what revelations have been made regarding that system in Washington into Wall Street, all the errors that have crept into it, political interference, and so on. One has only to read the report of proceedings -in the United States senate to see what has been done over there, and we are imitating them.

Where does the taxpayer come in? We sit here as members of parliament and we have no more to say about the railway department than has the man in the moon. Over the head of parliament a committee was appointed. I attended one or two sessions to see what was going on; thinking a member of parliament might reasonably ask for a copy of the report in the committee of railways and shipping, I applied for one, and a gentleman named Thompson of the Canadian National Railways, who was one of the old regime chiefs of staff and splendour, refused to let me have it. Well, I do not want any favours; I know enough about the way in which the railway has been administered.
I contend that the present government has no mandate from the Canadian people to return to the old state of affairs in connection with the national railways. It was not the government's election platform that returned them to power, for they had a different platform in every province. The reason they were returned to power was not the reason given by the Prime Minister yesterday; it was as a fact the deep resentment which the people of the world had felt against all governments then in power the world over, a resentment which they shared with people throughout the world against all governments. And I submit that the people of Canada removed from office a government which had received cold storage of justice and regard from the electorate. If the government insists on our going back to the old condition of things, at any rate let them not call it public ownership; let them call it Canadian Pacific ownership, because that is all it has ever been. Under Sir Henry Thornton the management was one of the most politically-minded the world has ever seen, and one of the most inefficient and useless in Canada.

I have not the time to discuss the broad issue of the Canadian National Railways; everyone agrees as to its importance. I would, however, crave the indulgence of the committee while I read a resolution adopted at a meeting of the Bonaventure county council held in New Carlisle, Quebec, on March 9, 1932. This resolution will indicate the feeling of the people of that district with respect to the way in which the Gaspe railway has been administered under the present regime, and the hope which they cherish that a change will be made under the new system which is about to be inaugurated. I could take up a good deal of the time of the committee covering the whole history of the railway, but in this resolution I find a

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
concise statement of the facts. The resolution reads:
Whereas the federal government has purchased and taken over the railway known as the Gaspe branch lines and has made said branch lines a part of the Canadian National Railways; and
Whereas since acquiring said branch lines, the railway management has undertaken to remove from Gaspe, New Carlisle and Matapedia, all repair shops and terminal operations, and to establish said repair shops and terminal operations in the town of Camp-bellton, in the province of New Brunswick, to the great detriment of Gaspe, New Carlisle and Matapedia, and to the people in general in the counties of Gaspd and Bonaventure, and especially to those whose means of livelihood have been taken away by the removal of said repair shops and terminals; and
Whereas the reasons given by the railway management for these changes are economy and efficiency; and
Whereas after several meetings between the management and interested parties, the reasons given by the management were not substantiated but rather were shown to be without foundation; and
Whereas a meeting was held in Montreal, on May 15, 1931, where Sir Henry Thornton, president of the Canadian National Railways, gave definite assurance to a representative delegation along with federal members of parliament for the province of Quebec that these changes would not be made; and
Whereas four months after this assurance was given the terminal at Matapedia was closed without previous notice and terminal operations transferred to Campbellton, N.B., with a gradual removal of all repair shops and other works from New Carlisle and Gaspe to Campbellton, N.B.;
Therefore be it resolved that we, mayors from every municipality in the county of Bonaventure composing the county council, protest against these changes for the following reasons:
1st. That removal of repair shops and terminals do not make for efficiency or economy but rather for less efficiency and certainly greater cost in operations;
2nd. That removal of these repair shops and terminals from the province of Quebec to the province of New Brunswick is a serious infringement of the rights of this province, which has made valuable contributions in both lands and money for the construction of these lines, with the just expectation that all reasonable benefits obtained in the operation of said lines should be for the people of this province;
3rd. That the removal of these works and terminals is a direct violation of the tacit understanding and promise arrived at with Sir Henry Thornton, and shows a serious disregard for the rights of the people in the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure, and disrespect for the chosen representatives of the people of this province with whom said understanding was arrived at;
Therefore be it further resolved that we, the members of this county council for the county of Bonaventure, in regular session at New Carlisle, and representing the divers interests in every municipality throughout the county, place ourselves on record as being
opposed to the removal from this county and province of the railway repair shops at New Carlisle and terminal operations at Matapedia or anything else the removal of which would be detrimental to our communities, county and province, and do hereby urge upon the railway management the necessity of reestablishing as soon as possible all works and terminal operations that have been removed;
And be it further resolved that a copy of this resolution be sent to: The Honourable the Prime Minister, the Minister of Railways, Sir Henry Thornton, Honourable Doctor E. Paquet, Lucien Moraud, K.C., Henri Larue, M.P., and Mr. Beaudry Leman and Hon. Charles Marcil, M.P. of Bonaventure county, and E. A. D. Morgan, K.C.
Mr. Morgan was the Conservative candidate in 1930. Nothing has been done since the passing of this resolution except that the western terminus of Matapedia has been removed from the place where it has been located for forty years into the province of New Brunswick, so that the railway has to go thirteen miles backwards to reach Campbellton, to the great dissatisfaction of the community. I congratulate the Minister of Railways on bringing about this change, so that that part of the province of Quebec, one of the oldest parts of Canada, may obtain that fair treatment to which it is entitled.

I have listened wi th care and attention to what the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has just said. If I have gathered correctly what is contained in that memonaeduim, I think it is a very poor reason indeed for any changes to be made. The railways cannot be efficiently administered in a national sense if local considerations are always to have preference; you will have what may be called a patchwork railway across the whole dominion. I realize the hardships, speaking in a local sense, that may accrue to some part of the country when a transfer is made of certain shops from one place to another. But the question where those shops should be located is not a matter for local determination; it must always be one of which the directors or the board of trustees and the administrative officials should be practically the sole judges. I feel sorry in one way for the position in which the hon. member for Bonaventure and certain of his constituents find themselves, but that in itself is not a condemnation of what has been done either by the existing board of trustees or by the previous management of the Canadian National Railways. It is quite conceivable that from time to time, due to adjustments which must be made in the administration of the railways, hardships will be inflicted upon certain communities. From that point

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
of view every member of the house, I think, feels a certain sense of regret and commiseration for those so affected, but they may have to suffer in the interest of the general benefit accruing to the railway system as a whole. What the hon. member for Bonaventure has said is true regarding not only the Canadian National system but the privately owned railways, and that condition will continue to arise from time to time when changes are necessary to bring about a fairly efficient management of the railroads of Canada.
It appears to me that in the course of discussion this afternoon we have been going, somewhat like the song, round and round. On this clause we have discussed virtually the whole railway situation as it affects the country at this time. Remarks of a general nature have been made with regard to how the railway should be run, the kind of equipment it should have, and so on. I believe that every one of the problems raised on the floor of the house this afternoon has also been raised from time to time in the committee which has been studying the railway question. I do not think this parliament or this committee as a whole is more competent in that regard than is the management of the two railroads or, specifically, of the Canadian National Railways. We have listened also to a great deal of talk about politics. That is quite the usual thing in this chamber when we discuss railways. I remember very well just a few years ago, when the former government took action which resulted in the dismissal of the late Sir Henry Thornton, and when the new setup of the railways was made, we had the cry of political interference with the Canadian National Railways. To-day, with the situation reversed, we have it again. I do not believe that in the proposed new setup, about which I am not in the least enthusiastic, we shall have any more political interference than we have had during the last five or six years. Last evening some fairly harsh things were said, particularly by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Caban), predicting political interference with the national railways as a result of the proposed new scheme. I do not share in that regard the fears of my hon. friend, but I take some exception to the government's action, and I do so on the ground I indicated last night when I spoke on this question for a minute or two.
When the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) discussed this clause of the bill he confused two aspects of the question, the first being its political significance, and

the second, the personnel. To my mind the two are entirely separate. I quite agree with the Prime Minister in his statement that the section contained in the act which this bill seeks to amend did convey to the existing board of trustees a power greater perhaps, than they should have had, because in case there was dissatisfaction in this house with the activities of the board it would have 'been a very difficult thing to remove them from office. It may be that far more powers were given to them than could be justified, or were contained in previous acts of parliament. On the other hand, the extent of the powers conferred by the act has really nothing to do with the personnel of the commission, and the objection I take at this time is to the very dangerous principle, which may become a bad precedent for future years, that whenever we have a change in the political complexion of parliament we are to have, or are likely to have, a new board of trustees. I very strongly object to that. As has been pointed out, I believe by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh), there is a great deal of dissatisfaction among the employees of the railway at the action this parliament is taking. Similar dissatisfaction was expressed when, in 1933, a similar bill was before the house. Now, three years later, we hear the same rumblings from the employees of the Canadian National system because of the changes that are being introduced in this house. I see, Mr. Chairman, that it is six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member has about half a minute more.

Mr. Chairman, you have become so exacting in looking at the clock that I think, if you will now give another look at it, you will probably say that it is six o'clock.
At six o'clock- the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

At half a minute to six o'clock when I asked for the recess I was discussing certain aspects of this question. I never knew that half a minute was quite so valuable. I know it is valuable when you have to catch a train; I know also many a half hour has gone without much serious work being done in this chamber. However I want to discuss one or two aspects of the clause at present before the committee. I hope that when the appointments to the directorate

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
are made by the government, they will obtain the very best men, irrespective of previous political convictions. It has, perhaps, been a weakness in former appointments that the political relationship of the appointees was a factor in making the selection. I hope on this occasion the only thing that will be taken into consideration will be the fitness of the men for the very responsible positions they will assume. I also ask that there be appointed from among the railway workers some man who has a practical knowledge of the railway men's side of the situation. I would prefer that the railway men themselves should have an opportunity of nominating either one man or a slate of three or four from which the government might make the appointment.
That brings me to the other question, which I suggested yesterday evening. If the government follows the practice of previous governments in choosing the men, it is quite likely that if at the next election there is a change of government the men now appointed to the responsible position of directors of the national railway system will be supplanted. I think that should be obviated. When a man has served a term as director or trustee he has gained experience which ought to be of value in the performance of his duty. If such a person has given good service it is a pity that the value of that experience should be lost. As the government insist on obtaining control of the Canadian National Railway system they should have adopted the same policy in this matter that they are following in connection with the Bank of Canada. To gain control of the bank directorate they are acquiring fifty-one per cent of the shares. It might have been a good precedent if in this case the government had nominated four new directors to be added to the three already occupying the position. However, as the government have thought otherwise, and the resignations of the chairman and board of trustees have been requested, I assume it is the intention of the government to appoint seven new men. I should like to hear from the minister his opinion of the suggestion I made last night, that there should be some agreement between the leaders of the different groups in this house as to the men to compose the new board of directors, so that there would be at least some assurance of permanency to them once they are appointed. I make that suggestion in all seriousness. There is nothing new in it; it has been adopted in many other spheres of public activity in this country, and there is no good reason why it should not be followed on this occasion. I do not say
that the nominations should be made from the floor of this chamber, but I would like to have the leaders or representatives of the various groups get together and see if they could not agree on seven suitable men to direct the affairs of the Canadian National Railways. That, I think, would be far preferable to the government having to assume the whole responsibility for the appointments. If the appointments were made in that manner we should be likely to get a better type of men for the position, as they would have some assurance of permanency.
During the afternoon some allusions were made to the matter of pensions or retiring allowances for the men who, through coordination of services, might lose their positions. The same question was raised in this house in 1933 when the act now being amended was before us. The .former government declined at that time to accede to that request. I am glad to see that on this occasion there are members of the Conservative party who favour such a proposal. When we come to discuss section 4 of the present bill I intend to move the same amendment as I did three years ago, asking for some form of compensation to be awarded to employees who lose their positions as a result of cooperation between the railways. I hope that when that time comes the proposals I make will receive the same sympathetic consideration by hon. members who spoke this afternoon. Good reason has already been given why such a proposal should receive sympathetic consideration. I think when the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe) was before the railway committee on Tuesday morning, he said that when the present chairman .of the board of trustees was asked to resign provision was to be made for a retiring allowance to him. If that can be done for the chairman of the board of trustees there is no reason why similar action should not be taken in regard to men who suffer the loss of their employment as a result of the present legislation. In the United States an agreement has recently been reached between the railways and. the employees whereby those who lose their employment as a result of coordination of services in that country receive compensation. That was a voluntary arrangement entered into between the unions and the managements of the roads. But that voluntary arrangement was brought about by the fact that in the United States congress legislation was pending which would make such compensation compulsory for the men who would lose their positions as a result of a process of amalgamation of services. So I
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

hope that when the time comes in this chamber for us to discuss the matter, both the government and the house will be sympathetic towards such a proposal, and that compensation will be provided for the men who lose their positions as a result of legislation such as that which we are now considering. There is a very good reason why we should do this. The men who may be affected by the legislation will lose their jobs because of an act of parliament. From the very nature of the legislation we must assume a certain responsibility for those men who might lose their jobs as a result of our legislative action. Personally I would oppose any legislation which had not within it certain provisions that would provide for the men under the contingencies I have mentioned.
At this time I should like the minister to state whether the government would be agreeable to a proposal to the effect that the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways would be jointly appointed or agreed to by the various groups in the house. If that were done it would create a favourable impression not only on the board appointed but among people throughout the dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member's question may I say that the government will make the appointments and will accept full responsibility for so doing. In British parliamentary institutions it is an established practice that the government must take responsibility for its actions. I cannot think who would take the responsibility if three groups undertook to share it. It does not seem to me that such action would be fair to the people of Canada. I assure the hon. member that when appointments are made they will be made by the government.
As to compensation for dislocation may I say that in the present circumstances we find an extraordinary situation. On the one hand we are taking the railways from the government. We say that the government must not have anything to do with them in any shape or form, and must turn them over to trustees to operate. I understand that attitude perfectly. Since I have held office I have taken that attitude. Yet the same people who take that position come to the government and say: You must make agreements between the management and the men. Why? Eighteen months ago I attended a luncheon in Toronto at which the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway expounded the principle that compensation payments should be made to men displaced. At that time he was talking about unification, and spoke of that factor as an aid to such unification. Two or three days
[Mr. Hcaps.l
ago we went into committee and heard the statement of the chairman of the board of trustees of the Canadian National Railways, when he suddenly discovered the reason he had not made progress in two and a half years of cooperation was that no provision had been made for taking care of the men displaced.
The minister is not justified in saying that that was the reason given by the chairman for not making progress. He said that they had made substantial progress, but he threw that out as a suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Why did he not have such
provision made? Who was to do it, if it was not the chairman of the board of trustees? He is the man vested with supreme authority over the railroad. This agreement has been made in the United States, how? It has been made not by legislation, but by agreement between the managements and the men. Every phase of relations between managements and men has been worked out by committees of the two. That is the proper way to do this. In a measure of this kind, which sets up a management of railways to operate independently of the government, why attempt to make the government responsible for the negotiation of labour agreements between the railways and the men? That is not consistent with the purpose behind the legislation.

May I answer the minister briefly as to why the government should interfere in a question of this kind. By the very nature of this legislation we are interfering with the two railways. I say that through the legislation we are going to compel cooperation, and when you have a certain amount of cooperation of services of the two railways, as a result of such legislation we automatically displace men who have given long years of service to the railways. In other words, as a result of the legislative action of this body men will lose their position.
In regard to the position in the United States, it was the government of that country which practically compelled the railway companies to negotiate an agreement with the men, and the threat was held over the heads of those companies that unless an agreement was arrived at a bill would be passed whereby such compensation would be made compulsory. Had there been no legislation introduced into congress it is quite likely that today there would be no voluntary agreement between the railways and the employees. Those are the simple facts. If the government is not prepared to insert in the bill a clause along the lines I have indicated, would it not

C.AMi.-Board of Directors
do the same thing as was done in the United States, namely compel the railways and the employees to come together and by voluntary agreement provide such compensation as might be determined by a board.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have tried to sort out the ideas of hon. members, and I should like to ask the hon. member who has just spoken if, under the present trustees set-up, or under the new set-up, it would be a proper function of government to interfere between the management and the men. In other words, should we tell the management what to do with their men? I would like to know that.
We are doing it, as a result of this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No; the legislation does not change the cooperative clause, in any way. That was passed in 1933, and is still in the statute. This enacts only the clause which has to do with the set-up of the management.
Quite right. This is practically the act of 1933, and in 1933-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No; it is nothing of the kind. It is a bill amending the measure of 1933 in certain particulars.

Yes, quite right. May I say to the Minister of Railways that in 1933 we moved an amendment to the bill along those lines. I notice the Minister of National Defence shakes his head in disapproval of what I am saying.

Hear,
hear.
He did not speak in that way in 1933 when he sat on this side of the house.
I am just reading what I said.
The minister should read Hansard.
I am reading it now.
I have it before me.
I suggest that the minister should read Hansard of April 7, 1933, and see what he said at that time.
The same thing; quote it.
I say-
Would the hon. member please quote it?
At that time the minister was speaking to a point of order, and dealt with an amendment before the house. He spoke in favour of the amendment.
Preserving the order of the house.
But when it came to a vote, he voted for the amendment being put.
To allow discussion; that is all.
We know what that means; it is more or less of a subterfuge.
Order.
I should not have used that term.
On a point of order. The hon. member should not impute his own particular qualities to other members.
He was using that as a means of giving his real views to the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member withdraw?

I withdraw the first statement; I think the second one is quite in order. I was saying that at that time a good deal of sympathy was expressed by hon. members of the Liberal party, as it has been expressed to-day on both sides of the house, in favour of compensation for the men affected. I am not asking for anything new. It is only to give compensation to the men who will be affected. What is wrong with the principle? The only thing which I find the minister states is wrong with it is that we cannot compel an agreement between the railway company and its employees. We may not be able to compel it, but we can put such a clause in the legislation and make it effective. We tried at that time to establish the principle that the interests of the public and the welfare of the employees of the road should have prior consideration, should take precedence over the interests of the bondholders. For it will be remembered that the present leader of the opposition, then Prime Minister, said that in reality the road was owned not by the people of Canada but by the bondholders; that the road to-day was almost, as it were, in the hands of the receivers, some such phrase as that.
The point which my colleague was trying to emphasize a few minutes ago is that if employees of the railroads are to be turned off to effect economies under the new set-up they may suffer a great deal of hardship. We are trying to insist that those who in consequence of this change will suffer loss shall be recompensed. I think that is a reasonable proposal, and one that should be advanced at this stage of the bill. The principle of compensation has been recognized in other spheres of business. The state has interfered in a great many ways between employer and employee, seeking to safeguard the interests of the employed; and what I was trying to point out was that even in a country, namely the United States, where perhaps we think lower standards prevail, this principle has been recognized. That is all I want to urge

at this stage. I am not advocating any particular methods by which that principle might be put into effect. In the United States it was done through an agreement. In this country, as my colleague has shown, the necessity for some protection of the employees has resulted directly from legislation introduced into this parliament. The minister, when my colleague made that statement, objected to it. He pointed out that we were not altering a great many things in the act of 1933. That is true. But the act of 1933 was brought in specifically to secure certain economies. Those economies could be obtained only as wages were cut down or as certain employees were laid off. Under those circumstances we tried to introduce the principle of compensation. The situation has now changed to this extent, that the board now being set up is replacing the old board for the very purpose of more effectively securing the economies which, the minister states, the old board failed to achieve. For this reason, since the government seems to be intent on economies, we believe it is all the more necessary that the proper claims of employees should be recognized.
One of the railroads is a government concern. Surely all along we have recognized certain special responsibilities of parliament towards the Canadian National Railways. We have paid the deficits of that railway, and we have done so in order to help the bondholders. Some of us take the position that, if it is necessary for this parliament to come to the aid of the bondholders, it is surely just as necessary that it should come to the help of the railway employees, more especially as the legislation is put on the statute books to help the bondholders. Should provision for compensation be put on the statute books? Well, if we are to provide certain safeguards for bondholders there is no reason why we should not, at the same time and in the same instrument, provide for the interests of the employees. Arthur Meighen was Prime Minister, who enunciated that policy when he was in opposition, I cannot see why the legislation of 1933 which is now being repealed was brought down in this house by the late prime minister. lation of that day, but by it three gentlemen, called trustees for whom I hare great respect, were given charge of 25,000 miles of railway in this country, including the Canadian government railways and the Intercolonial railway which under section 145 of the British North America Act belongs to the crown. The Intercolonial railway by one stroke of the pen was taken from the people of the maritime provinces and placed under a board of management on which the people of the maritime provinces had no representation and were practically not consulted. I was astounded to learn in the railway committee that in the last annual statement brought down by the present board of trustees they showed a deficit of $5,285,373 on the eastern lines, a deficit of $360,334 on the Prince Edward Island car ferry and terminal, and a deficit of $41,791,000 on the system. During the time I had the honour of sitting in parliament from 1922 to 1925, it was arranged after representation to the late Sir Henry Thornton and the board, that there would be regions established, and regions were established. Members from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island represented to Sir Henry Thornton and the board of directors, on which sat the then Deputy Minister of Railways, the reasons why we in the east should have an Atlantic division. That Atlantic region was set up, but we were given only the brain and the body; its legs were cut off; the region stopped at Riviere du Loup instead of continuing on to Montreal, which was the western terminus of the Intercolonial railway. In the statutes to-day the provision is that the Intercolonial railway consists of the line from Halifax through to Ste. Rosalie or Diamond junction.
From 1867 for forty-three years we had "arbitraries" on that road, to use the terms of the Minister of Inland Revenue of a former government. He called them, in relation to income tax, "arbitraries," why? Because they were not rates based upon any scientific system of railway rates but rates made in order to permit us to get into the market of central Canada and take our place industrially in this dominion. That was the reason the Atlantic division was set up. But that Atlantic division was a disappointment; it is a disappointment to-day, and we insist that that Atlantic region shall extend from Halifax to Montreal. Leave it as the late Hon. Mr. Blair made it and Hon. Mr. Emmerson left it, a road that we were proud of, started in the early days of confederation and pushing on towards the great centres that developed rapidly in central Canada, as compared with us in the maritime provinces with a small territory and a country closed against

us to the south by a high tariff and where so many of our people went to live. We started out with a great disadvantage; we are under that disadvantage to-day, and unless something is done to remove it I say with all sincerity that the consequences may be serious. I may not live to see them; I expect my life is not going to be so long, but other men will see what will happen unless the government afford us some relief. I speak in criticism of the government of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, and I think we may well bury the differences that may have existed. At this session of parliament we may well set ourselves to the task of righting the wrong that has been done, and we should attempt to place the maritime provinces in a position in relation to the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec as favourable as that in *which the 'western provinces are to the centre of the dominion. All hon. members know the Drummond county railway was leased by the Intercolonial under the authority of the parliament of Canada and that afterwards it was purchased. In time we saw the trains leaving the city of Halifax and travelling through to Montreal. Later we saw the shadow of a great wrong coming down upon us, and the train was cut in two at Riviere du Loup. The feet were taken off the head and body, and the train crews had to sleep in cars at Riviere du Loup, so as to pick up the train at that point returning to Halifax. They did not go through to Montreal, as they had done formerly.
We in the maritime provinces have some rights. I stated once before in this chamber, and I repeat to-night that we were the hewers of wood and the drawers of water. The men who made Canada what it is to-day came from the east because there was no west in their day. If the brains of the east made Canada what it is, surely we are entitled to some consideration. Our little province by the sounding sea, the province with a magnificent maritime frontage and the harbour with which God and nature endowed us, should be given what it deserves, what is its right. If, when we entered confederation, we gave all these advantages to round out and to make Canada the nation she is, surely at this late date we are not to be told that we cannot participate in her development from the province of Quebec through to the great Pacific ocean. Surely we in the maritime provinces are not gradually to recede as does the tide and die of ennui; surely we are to be given our proper place in the dominion, and surely industries in the maritimes which could compete with those in the central and prairie
