Napoleon said that military genius was the thing which ruled the world. The statutes of 1933 made provision for the appointment of three trustees who would have supreme control over 25,000 miles of railway. They would be responsible to parliament and to the Minister of Railways only in so far as *the making of reports and voting of moneys for capital expenditures were concerned. Beyond that they would sit on their thrones, but to-day those thrones are tottering. They were placed in a position even higher than that of the chief justice and judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, our final court of appeal, who can be removed only through the passing of an address by both houses of parliament. Our judges are placed in that high position because we want to have them removed from the man on the street. They are placed in that high position because they have to deal not only with property but with the lives of individuals governed by the laws of Canada. Therefore they should not feel that they are under the control of the people or of parliament.
Such conditions, however, do not apply to the board of trustees, and when the leader of the opposition placed them in a position equal to that occupied by the supreme court judges, I strongly suggest that he was going too far. The people of Canada who are paying through the nose for these 25,000 miles of railway have no right to speak or to whisper into the ears of the management of the national lines to-day. I do not believe in the patronage system as it existed in the early days, and I think we have developed to a point where such a system in its entirety could not exist. When men are placed in public positions, mind their own business and do their duty they should be protected. I have always taken that attitude, and I take it here to-night.
I must say, however, that I am in favour of the repeal of the 1933 legislation for the reasons I have indicated. In giving my opinion I do not have to appeal to the judgment of the Prime Minister, or to that of the Minister of Railways and Canals or to that of the Bennett government who were responsible for the legislation. I ask the leader of the opposition only to read the reasons given by Sir Robert Borden and those which were
given by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen when prime minister to the effect that under no organization other than a board of directors representative of the whole of Canada would it be possible to maintain a railway system in the interests of the people as a whole.
Some of the wrongs that have been done by the act of 1933 cannot be righted. When we are talking about amalgamation between the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railways, I would ask Sir Edward Beatty and his board of directors what action they took in connection with the Crowsnest Pass Rate Act of 1897, and why the rate applied only as far as Megantic in the province of Quebec and was not extended to the port of Saint John, which was the eastern terminus of the then Canadian Pacific railway which was then being operated from Vancouver to that port. This rate, if fixed to Saint John, would be met by the Canadian National Railways over their line to the port of Halifax and both ports would then come into their own in eastern ports.
If amalgamation is in the air, it will stay in the air. It will never come down to mother earth because there is no honest, sincere intention-I am not speaking now as to personal integrity-of doing anything at all to help the people of the maritime provinces on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but rather they wish to help themselves. They took advantage of the fact that as Megantic was the last point in eastern Canadian territory in the province of Quebec, before running across the state of Maine, they would not have to give the through rate which the Crowsnest pass agreement required. The railway as it existed and was operated in 1897-and they were operating in 1897 from Vancouver to Saint John-cut us off at Megantic, and they will as occasion requires cut us off at any other point. These great corporations have received much at the hands of Canada. A few millions of people have undertaken tremendous financial obligations, and in the words of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada in 1925, Sir Lyman Duff: This question was one that should be considered by itself on application to the court because it was not one of the questions for presentation to the supreme court at that time and therefore they were unable to pass upon it. But in the statutes to-day there is a provision sufficiently large.
There are 470 million bushels of wheat grown in our western country, and I would ask how many hundred millions of bushels of that wheat come through to the maritime ports in winter, either to Saint John or to

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
Halifax. It goes to Montreal and Quebec and is taken down the mighty St. Lawrence, and then when providence closes that great river by ice, where do these millions of bushels go? They go to United States ports, to be handled by the labourers and stevedores and agents in those ports, while the people who have spent almost their life-blood in order to survive and keep Canada together have to sit back and see their eastern gateways receiving nothing, practically doing nothing, and the port of Saint John would not be receiving what it is to-day if it were not for the fact that it is what you might call the half-time servant of a halftime corporation, the Canadian Pacific Railway, in this country.
Look back over what Canada has given the Canadian Pacific Railway, what wealth of money and wealth of soil; compare that with what the Canadian Pacific Railway is giving us, and then consider whether or not a few hundred thousand dollars thrown at the people of the maritime provinces is sufficient. It is like giving a milk bottle to a baby to keep it from crying when people are around and do not want to hear the noise, but when they go away the milk bottle is taken away and the baby can cry as long as it likes. We are not babies in the maritime provinces. We do not cry. We stand on our own ground, equal in status in Nova Scotia with the people of every other province of Canada, equal in status as completely and as securely as is Canada in the commonwealth of nations, under the act that my right hon. friend recommended in England be placed on the statute books there, the statute of Westminster, which makes all dominions of the empire equal in status. When we in Canada get that idea of the smaller eastern provinces having their rightful place and their proper share in the production, and distribution of the products of this dominion, thee we shall begin to feel that we are coming into our own, and tardy though it may be it is not yet too late.
I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister, the Minister of Railways, and the government on the step they have taken in this legislation. In the province in which I had the honour to be a candidate of the party supporting the right hon. the Prime Minister, one of the issues was the taking away of the power given to the board of trustees under chapter 33 of the statutes of 1933, the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, and putting it back where it rightfully belongs, in a board ol directors to be appointed by the governor in council, which exists through the authority of the people.
(Mr. Finn.)
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister was a bit too modest while speaking yesterday afternoon. In that great city of Toronto from where my hon. friend, the ex-mayor of Toronto, comes who spoke this afternoon (Mr. Church), where, it seems, there is neither liberty of thought nor liberty of action nor liberty in religion, no liberty perhaps in anything at all, the present Prime Minister, leader of the Liberal party, during the election campaign made this statement: "I desire the people of Canada to know that if I come into power-and I ask for a majority sufficient to give me a mandate to meet the senate which is overwhelmingly Conservative, so that they dare not touch legislation passed by the House of Commons of Canada through the people's will-I propose to repeal the 1933 act and go back to the system that we had before." That voice was heard clearly from one end of Canada to the other, and what was the answer? The answer is in this chamber to-night; it is in the representation behind the Prime Minister in this chamber to-night, the greatest representation ever given to a public man in Canada since Canada became a confederation in 1867. If my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition feels that he is being criticized inferentially through the repeal of the 1933 legislation, it is the will of the people as spoken at the polls as clearly as the voice of the right hon. gentleman or of the Prime Minister is heard in this house when they speak on questions of importance and on matters involving the future prosperity of this country.
Let me say further, Mr. Chairman, that before the railway committee I asked a question or two. I said: I notice that in your annual statement you have "eastern lines." There are not any. I asked: Is that the Atlantic division or region? The answer was, no. I said, " What does it include?" They told me that it included the road through to Ste Rosalie, outside Montreal and two pieces of railway in Quebec, one 180 miles long and the other 110 miles. I was told that that together with what is known as the Intercolonial railway makes up what they call the eastern lines on which they say there was $5,265,373.20 of a deficit. I asked if they would give me-this was on the order of the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset)-the receipts and expenditures on the Atlantic division as it existed to-day. Mr. Fairweather, who is in charge of the finances and economics of the road, said that it would cost too much to get that statement ready to let the people of the maritimes and of this country know how much it was costing to run the Atlantic division and how much was

being received in return. I want to be fair to Mr. Fairweather, to the president, Mr. Hungerford, and to the board of directors, but the fact remains that when the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) asked a question with reference to the deficit of some $383,000 on the Prince Edward Island ferry, in the twinkling of an eye, not waiting for the last trump or the last trumpet, they had the number of cars carried, the number of passengers carried and the cost of operating the nine miles of railway in Prince Edward Island. But they had no information to give the committee or parliament as to the cost of operating the Atlantic division, or how much of that deficit of over five million dollars belonged to the Atlantic region and how much belonged to what is known as the eastern lines of the Canadian National Railways.
In answer to an order of the chairman of the committee, Mr. Fairweather addressed to me a letter which speaks for itself. If an hon. member of this house is not entitled to information upon the order of a chairman of the committee so that he may deal intelligently with the question involved, then responsible government is gone. This is the first reason why the board of trustees should go. These officials have done as they pleased and they give just what information they want to give. You cannot find out what salaries they receive as it is shown in a lump sum. They are like certain other people; they go aside and they divide the loaves and the fishes. This is the letter I received. It is on the letter head of the Canadian National Railways, Bureau of Economics, Montreal, Quebec. It is dated May 8, 1936, and is addressed to me. This letter reads:
I did not have the opportunity of seeing you before leaving Ottawa. I recalled having promised to prepare a statement-

speechtext: I do not like to inter-dupt the hon. member, but he has spoken forty minutes.
I am sorry my forty minutes are up, but I am glad there are other sections.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was hoping
the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) would be in the chamber to-night. In connection with an answer which he made to me yesterday afternoon, I have gone into the record more carefully. The right hon. gentleman was referring to 1933 when section 7 of the existing act, which it is proposed to repeal, was under discussion. He stated:
I think it was stated very plainly that if that clause did carry, every effort would be
C.N.R.-Board of Directors
made to see that the House of Commons, which was the representative of the people as a whole, would not have its hands tied with respect to the control of any industrial activity for which it might be held responsible.
I have looked very carefully through the debates. I may have overlooked something but I cannot find anything which fully substantiates that remark of the Prime Minister But I should like to call attention to something that I did find. I refer hon. members to page 4583 of the Hansard of May 4, 1933. At that time the leader of the opposition of that day, the present Prime Minister, proposed that certain words in section 7 of the bill then under discussion should be struck out. This section reads:
No trustee shall be removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
The record shows that the present Prime Minister was then proposing to strike out from this section the words, "and on address' of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada." The section would then have read:
No trustee shall be removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause.
In moving that amendment the right hon. gentleman said:
-if any time a Liberal administration should be returned to power and I had anything to do with it, my last desire would be to remove any trustees appointed by the present government provided they were performing their duties impartially, fairly and well.
In reply to that statement, the then Prime Minister, the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), is reported on page 4585 of Hansard as follows:
When we say that good cause must be assigned for their removal or dismissal I am glad to hear the right hon. gentleman say that he thinks that is fair.
Mr Mackenzie King: I agree with that entirety.
I was intending to call the attention of the Prime Minister to those remarks. At that time he gave what was practically a pledge to the House of Commons that no trustees would be removed except for cause assigned. That statement "for cause assigned" has a very clear and specific meaning. If that pledge is to be carried out in its entirety, as I think it should be, the present trustees should not be removed except for cause assigned, at least for cause assigned to this House of Commons or to a committee of this House of Commons, so that the trustees who are about to be removed might have

CJSt.R.-Board oj Directors
ample opportunity to vindicate their position. I regretted very much, on reading the report of the standing committee on railways and shipping, which is now on the table of the house and therefore may be referred to by members, to learn that before that committee full opportunity was not given to its members to elicit the actual facts with regard to the proposed removal of the trustees, which was then under consideration.
With regard to the report made by Mr. Fullerton in reply to certain statements which have been made in the house by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe)-I believe it was on the second reading of this bill-Mr. Fullerton said:	,
I wish to say most emphatically that we have exerted every effort to vindicate the hopes of the commission, and to add with some pride that, having regard, to the brief time so far elapsed, we have achieved a substantial measure of success. So far as I have ever heard, there has not even been an allegation that the board of trustees has been influenced in the slightest degree by any political consideration at any time. The board has acted at all times, or endeavoured to act, as business men of broad and far-reaching responsibilities would act.	_
When we entered into office there had already been some years of the depression, and already great and needed economies had been put into effect, but under the management of the trustees these economies, in spite of obvious difficulties, were augmented, and to-day, when all the factors affecting the railway are taken into consideration, it is my confident claim that the railway is more economically operated, that its efficiency as a transportation system is greater, and that it is better equipped, from the viewpoint of prospective profit, to deal with business expansion than it ever was before. The proof of these claims will be found in the public records of the company.
I have been reading from page 216 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence before the standing committee on railways and shipping. I wish to do full justice to the Minister of Railways, for before the committee he stated very clearly, as reported at page 228:
I am willing to grant all that Judge Fullerton says about economies. I think the road has been carefully operated....
And so on. It seems to me under the circumstances that the pledge-because I think it was a pledge-made by the present Prime Minister when the original bill was under discussion, that none of these trustees would be removed from office by any government with which he was connected, unless for cause assigned, demands that before this bill finally passes there should be an opportunity for this committee of the House of Commons and for the House of Commons as a whole to ascertain definitely in what respect these

trustees have been delinquent in regard to the duties imposed upon them; otherwise they should not be removed. This house should be fully informed. Mr. Fullerton declared that in no case had any suggestion been made of any partisan action on their part, and I think that is entirely in accordance with the facts. He also stated that in dealing with the administration the commission had always sought what they believed to be the promotion of the best interests of the railway and of the public service as a whole. I think, therefore, that this house is entitled not only to have a cause assigned but to have full access to the evidence on which any complaint against these commissioners is based, so that the house itself, irrespective of any action that may be taken in another place, can fully and fairly consider whether these commissioners have been so delinquent in the administration of their office as to be subject to summary removal, as is proposed in this bill.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I desire to add only one or two words to what has been said by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I would point out first that it is now quite clear, from the statements made by the Minister of Railways, that this legislation is introduced into this house for the purpose of dispensing with the services of the present trustees. In his initial statement the minister made that fairly clear. If that statement is supplemented by the statements which he made in the committee, the evidence now being tabled in this house, it is quite clear that this measure is attributable to the fact that the trustees did not resign, as suggested.
The second point to which I desire to direct attention is that the minister aparently discussed with the chairman the conditions under which he might resign. Either the minister misunderstood the chairman or the chairman misunderstood him, for I assure him there was no discussion as to the chairman being appointed to any office under the late government in the event of his terminating his services. He took his superannuation allowance; before he took over the duties of chairman the order in council was passed by which he became a superannuated judge, and the question of appointing him to any position on the bench was never discussed as a possibility, although. it is just possible there may have been some laughing reference to the fact that he was giving up his position in the railway commission to the uncertainties of what might transpire in the event of there being a change of government. But no discussion ever took place looking towards his

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
appointment to the bench, my personal view being that a superannuated judge was not eligible for reappointment to the bench, having regard to the custom and practice under the constitution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Was he
appointed a judge under the old law prior to 1920?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He had
a right to superannuation after fifteen years.

Yes, quite so. Now, I do not think the minister discussed this with his law officers or he would realize the implications of any discussion of the kind to which reference was made in the testimony adduced before the select committee. It is a well known fact that the decisions of the courts in that regard are very, very striking. In Britain a public office is a public trust. The holder of that office cannot agree to terms under which he will accept resignation and have any claim in consequence of that contract vindicated or *made good in any court of justice. I looked up roughly, in view of the statement made by the minister, one or two decisions. One of them- was the case of a gentleman who possessed an office of importance in a dockyard. His friend suggested to him that he should accept his superannuation and retire on the usual pension, and in that case the friend would succeed him and allow him a certain annual share of the profits of the office. This agreement was carried out up to the point of there being a superannuation and an appointment, but after the friend received the appointment he was not disposed to pay the money. Thereupon the former officer brought his action, but the court held that he could not succeed; that an action could not be maintained on an agreement such as that, because a public office was a public trust, and that it was against public policy for any such action as that to be taken. Now, Judge Fullerton is an eminent judge and a very able lawyer, and I assume he knows the law far better than I do. But when I read the statement made by the minister in the committee I realized that possibly he had not consulted bis law officers or he would have been advised as to what the position is. That is the second point to which I desire to direct attention.
I am not going to amplify the third point, because it has been so fully dealt with by my hon. friend (Mr. Cahan) who has just spoken. He has gone with care over the records of Hansard. It will be observed that there was common ground between the then opposition and the government that these trustees should
be appointed for long terms and that the office would be vacated only for cause assigned. "Cause assigned," as the hon. member who has just spoken points out, is a cause given and stated by the person exercising the dismissing power. But that is not sufficient. Those of us who as students of our constitution recall the earliest cases to which attention was directed remember that an eminent judge in one of the colonies got into financial difficulties and was unable to pay his obligations. He gave promissory notes, which were very frequently renewed, and as a matter of fact, when he was sued on his notes, there was difficulty in connection with the carrying on of the proceedings in his court. Thereupon he was dismissed. My hon. friend from Cape Breton North-Victoria (Mr. Cameron) remembers the case of Graham v. Laffitte. The privy council held that Graham was properly dismissed in so far as there was ample cause to justify his dismissal, but that the dismissal was illegal, and he recovered. He succeeded in his action, why? Because he had not had an opportunity to be heard. When a man is appointed a judge for life his position is terminable only on address of both houses of parliament. That, at least, is the method adopted. He must have an opportunity to be heard. He must meet the assigned cause, and, meeting the assigned cause, he must be in a position to give his answer. If the answer is adequate, the cause is not sufficient; if the answer is inadequate, then of course the power is properly exercised. In this case, to my surprise, in view of the discussion which took place in this house at the very inception of this legislation, when I stated that I thought the chairman should have a chance to be heard and that that chance would come only when the committee met, I find the chairman taking the view that he should not be heard at all. Finally, however, it was arranged that he should make a statement. He made a statement in writing. Thereupon the minister of the day made the observation to which my friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has referred. On that statement, clearly, the chairman could not be dismissed. In other words, he has stated how he discharged his duties, and the minister has indicated that he has accepted that statement. The other two were not afforded an opportunity to be heard in the sense-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They refused.

Allow me to finish-in the sense of having charges alleged or causes assigned to which they could direct an answer. It is a fundamental principle that where office is held for a term which is terminable only for cause assigned, there must be the formal

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
proceedings for which the law provides if there is the termination, of that employment by the employer. And as I have pointed out, the law goes so far as to provide that, a public office being a public trust, it is not competent to negotiate legally with that person for what sums of money he will accept the termination of his employment, but that matter must be dealt with under another branch of law.
That establishes clearly, and without any question, I think, that by this legislation an attempt is being made to railroad the trustees out of their office by an enactment which is certainly at variance with the fixed principles upon which the legislatures have heretofore proceeded. In the Reilly case it was held, following an old decision, that those who hold office, civil or military, under the crown, hold office during pleasure, and the crown may terminate their employment, but there were special circumstances referred to in the case, which came up from Australia and has been frequently cited since, to the effect that if a contractual relation exists between the parties then the power to terminate at pleasure is gone. Here not only had we the contractual relation established, for a term of years, but we had the then leader of the opposition making a statement, which the then leader of the government said he regarded as a fair statement, indicating that the good faith and the high honour of parliament, at least as represented by the House of Commons, had been pledged to that course of action being pursued, namely assigned cause, which involves the opportunity of being heard, which in turn involves the cause being mentioned, for it must be assigned against him. And it is no good to deal in innuendoes, or in insinuations, or in inferences; you must deal with direct statements which constitute assigned cause in order that the action shall be taken.
So we have here, Mr. Chairman, a situation that I regard! as one to which the law officers of the crown should direct very careful consideration! and attention. The basis of this legislation fails. Its foundation has been destroyed by the minister in his first statement and in the statement he subsequently made in the committee, and, based upon our conception of British fair play, we are indebted for its application to this case to the pertinacity of my colleague the member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart), who succeeded in overcoming the attitude of the chairman and others that he should not be heard, and who deprecated the discussions that did take place. Therefore this must be regarded as the position: By common consent the trustees

could be removed only for cause assigned; no cause has been, assigned, and to the extent that there has been any discussion that discussion resulted in the alleged cause being held by the representative of the employers to be wholly inadequate. That is the position. On that state of affairs we are asked to repeal the legislation that appointed the trustees; we are asked to terminate their office without any suggestion of compensation; we are asked, without cause assigned, without an opportunity being given them to be heard, against their will to terminate their employment and dismiss them from the service of the country. Stripped of incidentals that is the case. I cannot add to the strength of what has been said by my colleague the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, but I hesitate to believe that a Canadian parliament is to set up this precedent. I hesitate to believe that when there was a consensus of opinion between the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and the then leader of the government who now stands here, as to the fairness of the attitude taken in the legislation, this parliament is to create such a precedent.
I quite understand the argument made yesterday by the Prime Minister as to the senate not being concerned. But the answer to it is one that perhaps does not suggest itself to the layman at first; it is this, that when we say that a man shall be removed from office on an address of parliament, that means both houses of parliament, because parliament does not consist of the House of Commons; it consists of the House of Commons and the Senate and the crown, in parliament assembled. That is the reason our legislation runs in the terms that it does. The senate is introduced into the legislation by name because the senate house of parliament is a constituent house of parliament, this being the commons house of parliament, and the two houses together make up the parliament of Canada. That is why the legislation is drawn in the terms in which it is. The argument that was made by the Prime Minister respecting the right of the senate to deal with matters affecting taxation is, of course, rather an, old argument and is based upon the sound principle, by analogy, that the House of Lords in Great Britain has not the right to deal with matters affecting taxation and revenues, money bills as it is put. But the late Senator Ross was of the opinion, after a careful review of the authorities, that that power was possessed by the Senate of Canada. That is not a matter which need

CJV.E.-Board oj Directors
concern us at the moment; it is sufficient for my purpose to point out that the reason reference is made to the senate in the section which is to be repealed is that the senate is a constituent house of the parliament of Canada, and that reference is generally made to addresses being made by both houses of parliament rather than by one.
So far as this legislation being conceived as a Tory plan, if hon. members read again the words of the Prime Minister to which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George referred, I think they will realize that at that time the Prime Minister did not so consider the legislation. Although many things were said about it, and will continue to be, the fact is that in that instance there was apparently a common understanding. I said that I thought the statement he made was a fair one, and I repeat that I think it was a fair one.
The question of minorities and majorities was raised. Of course changes of government have always brought about difficulties. Where those who formerly sat in opposition are in office and those who were in office are in opposition, there is a tendency on the part of the new government to try to make good the position they took in opposition. But there have been exceptions to that rule. The law and the custom of the constitution are predicated upon an entirely different conception of the situation. If hon. members read the parliamentary history of Great Britain they will find successive governments under Mr. Gladstone continuing to maintain legislation which was passed by their Conservative predecessors. It will be recalled that with respect to reform measures, to the com laws, to much other legislation, notably the unemployment insurance act in recent times, new governments have maintained the legislation of their predecessors. Frequently they have made changes and additions for the purpose of making it more in accordance with their conception of its usefulness, but they have maintained it. Here we have an illustration of a situation that has grown up markedly since my hon. friends assumed office. Men were appointed to positions for a period of five years. Then they were told that they held office during pleasure, and were dismissed. Of course I would say that that question may have to be settled ultimately by a court. The judgment in the Reilly case makes it quite clear that if the court should find that there is a contract, then the rule with respect to service to the crown, whether military or civil, being service during pleasure would not prevail; the ordinary rule of contractual liability on the part of those who without cause terminate an agreement of
service or of hiring would prevail, and damages would be recoverable. In the Reilly case the court took the view that as the man could no longer offer himself for the discharge of his duties because the office no longer existed, he could not recover damages, and they avoided determining the question whether or not a contract existed.
I submit to this committee that, by the course the government propose to follow, we shall be creating a very dangerous precedent. It is a course of legislation which is at variance with all our precedents, and is in my judgment wholly unworthy of this house or of the government of the day. I mention it only in this sense because, when I read the statement made by the chairman of the trustee board, Judge Fullerton, and the statement made by the minister, added to what he said on a previous occasion, I realized that this is what has sometimes been described in the courts as mere brute force. It is a case of abolishing a position for the purpose of getting rid of the present incumbents. I submit that is not a proper course to follow and cannot but be injurious to the well-being of this country.
One word more upon the other questions discussed this afternoon. I am wholly in accord with the minister if he says that in his judgment as the new minister it is desirable to remove the veto power of the chairman. I am not going to quarrel with that, if the minister says that he considers it desirable in his interest to have that veto power done away with. It was inserted in the act because the commission thought it desirable that it should be there. The question of continuity, the question of permanency, the question of creating a policy and outlining a policy-all these are matters with which the commission dealt, and I have referred to them in previous statements to the house. I shall not weary the committee by making further reference -to them, more than to say that they constitute the causes which led up to the recommendations for the legislation.
Without going into the matter in detail may I say that if the minister, especially one who has accepted great responsibility, thought it desirable to improve or make more workable some condition, or to bring about a more direct relationship between the government and the commission, I could quite understand his introducing such legislation. But when the avowed design of the legislation is to get rid of three men who occupy positions as trustees, and to substitute for them men called directors, with all the difficulties to which the commission has pointed out directors are subject, I suggest that this is not a proper course to take. I

C.NJI.-Board of Directors
say that, when I remember what directors have brought upon us in almost all parts of the country, whether it be in connection with the Vermont Central, with the Grand Trunk Western, with steamships or with some part of the country. No matter whether it was in Montreal or elsewhere, we had difficulties come to us by reason of the appointment and operations of directors. The reason was obvious, wholly obvious. I have heard nothing from the minister to indicate that those reasons will not continue. On the contrary, our old friend, one of the venerable and venerated members of this house (Mr. Marcil) only this afternoon read a petition in which he pointed out that in the interests of efficiency and economy certain changes were made with respect to railway workshops at a point where repairs were carried on. "In the interests of economy and efficiency" were the words used. A change was made from one point to another, namely from point A to point B, in other words to Campbellton rather than elsewhere. Just imagine the pressure that will be heaped up against these directors! This is a fair warning. Can the directors resist the power of 170 odd members of parliament? If the minister means what his words would seem to indicate, he is not going to have anything to do with the operation of the railways; that is going to be done by the president and directors. I may say that .if an examination were conducted on cause assigned I have no doubt the minister would discover many things he ought to know, because inevitably where you have a combination of both systems there are difficulties. The late Sir Henry Thornton found difficulties but he brought them into a harmonious whole. Now and then we find the assertion of this or that right on the part of the old road or one of the other roads, and the difficulty of creating harmonious operation of the system is very, very great.
In his statement Mr. Fullerton referred to that difficulty. But when there is a great depression and a lessening of traffic and revenue, with a consequent laying off of men, the human factor enters into the problem, and the consideration of that human factor involves many questions to which references have been made to-day. The essential point it seems to me we cannot get away from is that the very feature contained in the address made this afternoon in connection with the acquisition of branch lines, and other properties, in a constituency represented by a member on the government side of the house represents an effort which must and will be made to secure a recognition of local communities for local purposes as against efficiency and economy, which were the

grounds put forward by the late Sir Henry Thornton as the reasons for actions which were taken. That condition is going to be intensified one hundredfold. It will be intensified one hundredfold, under a board of directors.
The whole purpose of the Duff commission was to create a body just the opposite of a directorate. Why? Because this was a publicly owned property in connection with which the House of Commons had undertaken to represent the shareholders, and a property which, as I pointed out, if the ordinary rules of law were to prevail, would have been in the hands of receivers long since, and would have been operated for the benefit of those who held the securities. In order that we might avoid that, trustees were appointed. They were free from political consideration, and Judge Fullerton has accentuated that point in the statement he made. Others have done the same thing.
I know about all the complaints; I know about the complaints made. I know it was complained that these men would not take a political outlook. Do I not know, sir, the extent to which the late government suffered? Do I not know about the appeals that were made? Do I not know about the votes that were lost? Do I not know about the successful effort made to create poisoned ideas and views in the minds of Canadian National employees? Have I forgotten? I have not. I have not forgotten the propaganda and the efforts that were made. Are we to return to that? If we are not, then all I can say is that the minister must either yield or leave; no alternative is left, because of the very action that has been taken ever since the trustees took office.
In the very nature of things we must be sincere, whether we like it or not. In connection with this matter we must be sincere, and I cannot but think that hon. members of the committee must realize that the substitution of directors for trustees will bring about an inevitable recurrence of the difficulties to which reference has been made, and which were accentuated this afternoon by the observations of the hon. member for Bonaventure, when he indicated his position.
The statement of the summary of the Duff commission made by Judge Fullerton is so ample that I think not even the hardest cynic could object to its fairness. This is the last opportunity afforded in committee to raise our voices against the repeal of a statute which entrusted to a body of three trustees the administration of the greatest property the Canadian people own. If the minister is dissatisfied with the trustees I have no doubt methods could be devised by which they could

CJVJt.-Board of Directors
be replaced. To do it in this indirect manner is bad enough, but when for the trustees he substitutes directors, the very persons against whom the Duff commission reported, those persons because of whom the red line of extravagance was running through the whole operation of the system, then I say that he has invited the very criticism which has been made in this committee, namely that the action is taken for the purpose of restoring those days, with all the sad effects they have had upon the Canadian taxpayer.
That is the reason-I know it is too late- why I appeal to the minister to think carefully; I appeal to the Minister of Justice, too, to consider the precedent we are establishing with respect to the disposition of the trustees, realizing that a public office is a public trust. The approach which was made to the matter was unfortunate; I do not blame the Minister of Railways for that, because he is not a lawyer. But it is quite obvious that had he had brought to his attention the decisions of the courts with respect to the position in which Judge Fullerton would have placed himself had he yielded to any suggestions that he be provided with this or that office, with this or that position or with a sum of money, unless it be a sum placed in the estimates, the minister would run counter to this. He would have had regard for that great line of decisions which, strange as it may sound, began as far back as 1551, when a statute was passed in Great Britain. It has brought about other statutes and decisions since that time, and that is the reason why in Great Britain they could not possibly submit to parliament a measure such as this. It would fill British legislators with a sense of horror to have submitted to them a statute that proposed, without conferring an opportunity to answer to an assigned cause, to wipe out trustees in the method which is being followed in this bill.
I can only make this final suggestion-it will do no good, of course-as to the desirability of the government reconsidering the matter from the other angle which apparently they had not thought of at all until the statements made by Judge Fullerton and by the minister appeared. But now that they do appear, it seems to me that we have in the printed word reasons which should influence this committee, and the government first of all, to hesitate to ask the members to follow a course, pursue a policy, and create a. precedent which is without parallel, so far as I know, in the whole British empire, and which does violence to every settled and established rule dealing with the relations between the crown and its servants. For while Judge 12739-218
Fullerton and the trustees were paid by the railway company, they were appointed by the crown in the exercise of the power conferred by parliament, and when a contract such as that is made by the crown with its servants, to suggest that those servants should be treated in this way is, I say, doing violence to every established precedent. But worse than that, it creates a sense of unfairness and of injustice which, while it might meet with temporary cheers and approval, cannot in any sense be divested of its real quality if sufficient examination and analysis are given to the statute under which that power is to be exercised.
This section repeals the existing law. The government, I can readily understand, desire to make modifications and changes in this law as they have in other statutes, but so far as the general principle is concerned I hope that on reconsideration, and especially in view of what has taken place in the committee, the government will realize the desirability of not departing from known pathways of conduct and will not endeavour to establish a precedent that, in my judgment, will react some day or another, I do not know when, upon the heads of those who are responsible for it.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Part I.

I have an amendment, Mr. Chairman, to section 3, as follows:
That all the words after the word "council" in the third line on page six of the bill down to and including the word "approve" in the sixth line, on page six of the bill, be struck out.
These are separate sections, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I might explain that. Section
3 says:
Part I of the said acts is repealed and the following substituted therefor.

I was going to suggest to the minister, although of course it is not for me to say, that these paragraphs 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and so on down to 15, should have been designated by different figures because they

are not sections; they are really paragraphs, and might be designated a, b, c, and so on. The section is 3, but these paragraphs 4, 5, 6, and so forth appear in the bill as if they were separate sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, and I thought it well to direct attention to that. I think we should jertainly consider section 3 paragraph by paragraph, because in the act they will be separate sections.
The minister has stated it exactly. This section 3 repeals a whole part, consisting of several sections of the existing act.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

The proper way, I submit, to have done it would have been to repeal the old act section by section and substitute the new sections. This may have the same effect, but in consolidating the act later for office purposes these paragraphs 4, 5, 6, and so forth, must appear as sections of the new act.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite correct. We could have repealed it paragraph by paragraph, but the draftsmen have in fact repealed all of part I.
That is clear, and the following are substituted therefor. The question is how they shall be numbered.
Of course, we have been discussing section 3 of the bill. Section o is practically the whole bill, and therefore we were entitled to roam from Dan to Beersheba.

On section 3, paragraph 5-Remuneration of directors.

Has the minister any
statement to make as to the salaries it is proposed to pay the directors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I do not know that that has been considered. We propose to put this pretty much on the basis of national service, and not attempt to pay the class of men we hope to get for the actual time they spend. But I suppose quite a small sum, perhaps three or four thousand dollars.
Does the minister think he can get competent railway directors for three or four thousand dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think we can get men of the right type, anxious to do national service, who will put service above the actual remuneration.

Does the minister think it would be possible to get that type of man able to divorce himself from his own business to the extent of being able to meet with the board of directors once a week for the purpose of doing railway business?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I feel that we can. When I said three or four thousand dollars, I would not like to be tied to that, for it might be five or six thousand dollars; I would say not more than six thousand dollars, but that is a situation we have to meet when we come to discuss it with the men we hope to get. I do not think any man that we might hope to get will discuss salary until after he has decided whether or not he will accept the position.
The board of directors as suggested by the minister is to consist of seven members?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

One of whom will be the
chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Quite.

In the appointment of these directors is it the intention to carry out the principle and appoint a board of directors representative of the different parts of

Canada? I do not know whether the government has definitely made up its mind in this connection and if the minister cannot answer me to-night, I shall be quite satisfied to have his answer later before the bill is finally dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We shall decide what directors we shall get when the bill passes.

I must take issue with the minister. There is a principle involved in this change. A few moments ago I referred to the remarks of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen and the reasons he gave for appointing such a board of directors. He contended that politics would be removed and the board would be representative of the different parts of Canada; that they would know the local conditions and needs, the same as a doctor does when he visits the bedside of a patient. I am speaking only for my own province of Nova Scotia and hon. gentlemen who represent Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick can speak for themselves. I should like to know if this board of directors is to be representative of all the provinces of Canada. The minister now tells me that a statement will be made after the bill is passed and the stable door is locked. I think this committee is entitled to this information. We should know the type of man to be selected and whether territorial limits will be taken into consideration in the appointments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall paragraph 5
carry?

I think I am entitled to an answer from the minister, and if I am not to get one, I should like him to say so. I want to be fair, but I shall not, without uttering my protest, permit legislation, whether it be introduced by the government or otherwise, to pass that might be subversive to the best interests of the province which I have the honour to represent. I think, before this legislation leaves the committee, every hon. member present is entitled to receive the information he desires.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I want to give my hon. friend the fullest possible information, but I thought I made it quite clear that the government have not gone as far with the selection of directors as my hon. friend seems to think. They hope to get six men and a chairman who will be of the greatest value to the property. I can assure my hon. friend that when the time comes the considerations he mentions will be weighed very carefully, but surely he should not ask me at this time as to the policy of the government with reference to these directors who have not been definitely chosen.

Perhaps the minister has misunderstood me. I did not ask him who the directors were to be; I asked him whether in the selection of these directors the question of territorial limits would be considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

Paragraph 5 agreed to.
On section 3, paragraph 6-Tenure.

How does the minister propose to assure these directors that they will have continuity of office. Three of the original directors are to be appointed for three years; two are to be appointed for two years, and two for one year; then the succeeding directors are to be appointed for periods of three years. The present board of trustees were assured by statute of a term of five years. They have been in office a little more than two years and now they are being simply legislated out; the statute means nothing. What confidence can be placed in this statutory assurance of three year appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I may say that I do not consider that of the highest importance since the men who will be chosen will be selected because they feel they can make a contribution to their country. I believe that should there be a change of government and it is intimated to these men that they have not the confidence of the government, they will retire promptly. I would expect that men of the calibre we hope to get would do that, and I would be disappointed if they did not. In the meantime, they are to be appointed for three years, and one-third of the board retires each year. In other words, the board of directors faces its shareholders every three years just as is the case in many private corporations. I think that is a very proper thing and I would not care to do anything to tie the hands of the next parliament from reorganizing this board as they see fit.

I am referring to this
revision to the old system. It means that these directors are being appointed for the term of office of the existing government; that is the effect of the minister's observations. In other words, we are declaring to the country that in so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, its policy of operation, its policy of administration must be attuned to the policy of the government that happens to be in office. I think it is important that this fact should be recognized in passing this
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

legislation. In my opinion, it is possible to change that. Would the minister consider the suggestion of having these directors appointed by parliament itself, thus ensuring at least before any change is made, a full discussion by parliament acting as shareholders of the railway? For if the theory just expounded by the minister is to be the doctrine which will govern us, it really means that we are creating a partisan board of directors; that is what it amounts to. Altogether apart from what is in the minister's mind at the moment, this legislation as such will amount to a partisan appointment of directors. The minister has emphasized twice already, I believe, in the last few minutes, his hope of getting men who will serve the country and accept this office as a national service. That is fine, and I shall not, in anticipation, cast reflections upon these gentlemen; I have no doubt that very worthy gentlemen will be chosen. But the point is that behind it all we are adopting a system which will grow into and be perpetuated as a partisan administration of the railways. That is exactly what was intended to be overcome by means of the trustee system. I confess that when the legislation was first brought down, after the Duff commission had reported, for the appointment of trustees, I considered that that phase of the matter required a great deal of thought if its value was to be appreciated. But having seen it put into operation I have come to the conclusion that it was sound, not only as a method of getting away from the partisan element which inevitably creeps in, but in addition to that for the reason that the trustee system clothed the administration of the railways with authority in connection with dealing with the competing railway, which I think is impossible in connection with a board of directors. Well, I will not say impossible- that is going too far-but it could not be done with the same efficiency by a board of directors as by a board of trustees. In my opinion the minister should give this paragraph further consideration.
I would suggest that parliament might well consider now, if we are going to depart from the system of trustees, whether or not the directors should be appointed by parliament itself. That is a thought which has been in my mind many times in the past when this subject of the national railways has been before parliament. I have long had the view that it might be advisable-that is, when the railway was under a board of directors-that parliament might at some period of the session sit as shareholders of

the railway. We might constitute the house in committee of the whole as a meeting of shareholders for the purpose of appointing directors, receiving the annual statement and dispatching business of that kind. Parliament as a committee of the whole might sit as shareholders of the railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no provision
anywhere for parliament sitting as a committee of the whole.

No, but there is no
reason why parliament should not pass legislation for the introduction of that system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think it could
constitutionally. Parliament is composed of two bodies functioning separately, each within its own orbit.

There is no reason in
the world, however, why parliament could not pass a statute. I am not saying that my idea is the wisest; I am merely offering it as an opinion. There is no reason why parliament should not pass a statute providing that in so far as the national railways are concerned an annual meeting might be held which would be attended by all the elected members of parliament as representing the people, who are the owners of the property. As the company operates to-day, or as it will operate under this bill, it will be administered by a board of directors, and the only body above the board of directors will be the executive, namely, the cabinet or the government of the country. As a matter of fact, every citizen or taxpayer in Canada is a shareholder of the railway, but it is obvious that you could not have a meeting representing the shareholders as an ordinary shareholders' meeting is held. We could, however, enlarge the number by constituting parliament itself as representing the shareholders for the purpose of appointing directors and performing other limited duties. About three years ago, in 1933, we passed a statute which provided that the trustees should be appointed for a term of five years. They have been in office for something like two or two and a half years, and now by legislation we are removing them without any cause assigned. There has been no complaint; there cannot be any reasonable complaint sufficient to warrant their removal. We ar_ declaring in this bill that the directors shall hold office for three years. But there is no guarantee whatever that these directors will hold their office for three years.

Why not say for the duration of this parliament?

That would be a much
more frank way of putting it, because that is what it means. For hon. gentlemen at present on the government benches cannot now take an action that nullifies the action of parliament three years ago and say: We are so much superior to those who preceded us that any action we may take will stand and these directors will remain in office for the full term of three years. The government must expect that, once having established this precedent in connection with the national railways, other governments will be inclined to follow in their footsteps, and they would have abundant excuse for doing so. Personally I should like to see in this bill something repudiating the idea of interference with these appointees, once appointed, except for dereliction of duty or incapacity or untrustworthiness or something of that sort. That is the only reason why a man should be removed. I offer these suggestions for what they are worth.

We are providing in this measure that the governor in council shall be a shareholder of the company for all purposes under the railway act. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) has referred to members of parliament, the senate and the commons, voting as shareholders. It is quite competent for us to pass a statute to that effect. I at one time had a plan by which all the members of the local legislatures and of parliament, the senate and the commons, should cast a ballot for the election of the directors of this road, and should be authorized by parliament to act as shareholders for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should be interested to know the reason my right hon. friend abandoned the idea, to see whether it is the same reason that actuated me in abandoning a similar plan.

I abandoned it because
it did not appeal to those to whom I suggested it. I am going to be perfectly frank about the matter, because the minister was very frank this afternoon about his speech. I might say that the plan did not seem to win commendation from anybody.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had the same experience.

That is a fair statement of the situation. On the other hand the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has put his finger upon it. What this government
says is this: "We found a man who had a right to a job for five years, who was given that job by an act of the parliament of Canada; we wiped it out, and we are going to make the appointment for three years"-which makes it a joke. Why not say, "shall hold office during the lifetime of the present government," or "unless they change their mind," or "as long as their present state of mind continues?" Having said that there is no value to a written contract; that an act of parliament is a worthless scrap of paper, why not be consistent and put it in the statute? That is the position. The minister should be consistent about it. He has declared that a former act of parliament is a piece of waste paper. That act gave one man a position for five years, and others for a less time; one expires in December next. Why not say in this section, "They shall hold office as long as we think they should, and no longer," "we" meaning the present government? That would be better than coming down to this parliament and repudiating a statute. It would be much better to indulge in an act of acquiescence rather than in an act of repudiation, and simply to say, "We acquiesce in the position which we have taken and are going to embody in this statute a provision that hereafter no man may be appointed for three, four, five, six, eight, or ten years-that doesn't mean anything to us- but, so long as we feel he is satisfactory to us." It sounds so much better than to go through all these formalities about equity and fair dealing and doing justice and loving mercy, and the other clause that I shall leave unsaid. Why not do what I suggest? I am very serious about it. Having repudiated all these provisions of last year in the section, why not now say, "We will save parliament trouble by saying that the term shall be three years or such time as to the governor in council may seem satisfactory?" In other words, as long as the pressure from without is sufficient to enable them to discharge their duties to the satisfaction of the members of the House of Commons who sit to the right of the Speaker, it is all right. I suggest seriously to the government that they should put that on the statute book.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I may say, Mr. Chairman, that in 1933 for the first time legislation was passed which attempted to tie the hands of an incoming government beyond peradventure, by making a change of personnel possible only by means of a joint address of the Senate and the House of Commons. The present government is not perpetuating that method.

This bill can pass only with the consent of both houses of parliament.

Hear, hear.

You are in no worse position now than you would be under any circumstances in which you wish to repeal an act constituting the national railway board. You must now go to the other house and secure their consent to the bill which is at present before the committee. There can be no legislative measure without the consent, direct or indirect, of both houses of parliament, and when it is suggested that the address should be concurred in by the Senate and the House of Commons, that is the form provided by the rules of this house for every address which is to receive the approval of parliament for any purpose whatsoever.
Petitions have to go to both houses.

Would the minister allow me to ask a question regarding a paragraph that has already passed? Paragraph 5 of section 3 provides that the directors shall not be entitled to receive any other recompense of emolument from the Canadian National Railways or any company of which they form a part. Would it not be a good idea to provide that they should not receive any recompense or other emolument from any other railway company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think the hon. member can leave it to the good judgment of the government not to appoint directors or employees of other railway companies.

I do not mean directors or employees; I mean people who are under an obligation, possibly pensioners, or who are closely allied with them by way of having large business dealings with them and things like that. If it is desirable that they should be absolutely clear from the Canadian National Railways, it is ten times more so that they should have no connection, direct or indirect, open or concealed, with any other railway.
Will this be paid by the railway or by the crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: By the railway. The purpose of paragraph 5 is merely to provide that they will not get two or three emoluments from serving on different boards of the railways, of which there are so many boards. They are to be paid one fee by the railways.

The minister persists in stating or insinuating or suggesting that the object behind the fixing of the period of office of the trusteees was a political one; that it was done for the purpose of tying the hands of a succeeding government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: So it was.
The minister was not in the house at the time.

I ask the minister to read the report of the Duff commission and to study the reason why that commission recommended the appointment of a board of trustees and recommended also that it be given permanence.
And the length of time.
And the length of time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Did my hon. friends opposite adopt the length of time?

I do not know that we adopted the report in every detail. There were reasons given by the commission why trustees should be appointed and the desirability of their having a secure tenure of office, in order that one of the troubles which was referred to in the report might not occur again.
